cases.title: `^build` builds every dependency before the project that needs it
cases.why: A project’s build reads what its dependencies built, so each dependency must finish first. Started early, app concatenates a lib or ui output that is missing or left over from an older build. The run can still exit 0, so the bad bundle ships without anyone seeing an error.

cases.title: Running one project's task runs what it depends on, and nothing else
cases.why: Asking for one project’s task means that task done right, which needs what it depends on built first. Skipping the dependencies builds ui on a missing or stale lib. Running unrelated projects as well spends CI minutes on work nobody asked for and can fail the run on code the user did not touch.

cases.title: A bare name in dependsOn waits on the same project’s task
cases.why: A bare name in dependsOn points at a task in the same project, the usual way to say test needs build. If the runner ignores it or looks elsewhere, test reads a `dist` that is missing or from the last build. The test then passes or fails on old code, which is worse than no test.

cases.title: `lib#build` in dependsOn runs that task first, with no package dependency
cases.why: An edge like `lib#build` states an order the package manifests do not show. site publishes lib’s output, so lib must be built first even though site does not list lib as a dependency. Ignoring the edge publishes a missing or stale file, and the order would hold only by luck of timing.

cases.title: A dependency two projects share builds once per run
cases.why: When two projects depend on the same library, one run needs that library built only once. Building it twice wastes time, and a second build can rewrite files while the first consumer is reading them. Each task in a run is one unit of work, however many paths lead to it.

cases.title: A task only some projects declare runs in exactly those
cases.why: Running a task by name runs it where it is declared and nowhere else. A project without that task has nothing to run, and should not be swapped for some other task it does have. Running `build` in place of a missing `lint` does work nobody asked for and reports it as lint.

cases.title: A project whose directory holds spaces builds, caches and restores
cases.why: A directory name with spaces is a valid path and must work like any other. A runner that splits paths on spaces misses inputs, writes outputs to the wrong place or fails to restore them. The project then looks cached while its `dist` stays empty, or never caches at all.

cases.title: A task named `test:unit` runs as its own task
cases.why: A colon is a common part of task names such as `test:unit`, not a separator the runner may reinterpret. Reading it as project and task, or as a prefix of `test`, runs the wrong command. The user asked for unit tests and gets the whole suite, or nothing, under the same green exit.

cases.title: `^gen` runs the dependencies’ gen first, and not their build
cases.why: `^gen` asks for one specific task in each dependency, here the code generation app reads. Running lib’s build in its place leaves `gen/g.txt` missing or stale, and app builds on it. Running both wastes time on a build nobody asked for; the caret names a task, not a whole project.

cases.title: `^build` over a dependency that declares no build runs the project alone
cases.why: `^build` means build each dependency that has a build. A dependency without one has nothing to wait for, so the project runs on its own. Failing the run would make every project declare an empty build, and running some other task of lib in its place does work nobody asked for.

cases.title: A five-project chain builds strictly from the bottom up
cases.why: Each project in the chain reads the one below it, so the order must hold at every step, not only the first. If any build starts early it reads a missing or older output, and the error carries silently up to the top. A long chain is where a scheduler that only checks direct edges or races ahead shows it.

cases.why: Two selected projects that share a dependency need it built once, and before either of them. Building it twice wastes time and can rewrite its output while one of them reads it. Starting either project before the shared build finishes gives it a missing or stale input.

cases.title: `^build` follows a dependency by package name when its directory is named otherwise
cases.why: Projects depend on each other by package name, and the directory a package lives in can be named anything. Matching dependencies by directory name drops the edge from app to ui. app then builds before ui, or on an old ui, and the run still exits 0.

cases.title: `@acme/core#build` in dependsOn runs that scoped project’s build first
cases.why: Scoped names such as `@acme/core` are ordinary package names and must work in an explicit edge. A runner that misreads the `@` or the `/` cannot find the task and either fails or drops the edge. Dropping it lets site build first and copy a missing or stale core output.

cases.title: A project nested in another runs its own task in its own directory
cases.why: A project inside another project’s directory is still its own project with its own task. Running it from the outer directory, or folding it into the outer project, writes outputs to the wrong place or skips it. Each task must run where its project lives, or its paths mean something else.

cases.why: Packages that depend on each other form a cycle only for tasks that wait on dependencies. A task that names no dependency has no order to keep, so nothing stops it. Refusing the run would block checks like lint in any workspace with a package cycle, for no reason the tasks give.

cases.title: `^build` across projects that depend on each other fails before any build runs
cases.why: When each build waits on the other, no order is right: whichever runs first builds on a dependency not built yet. Running anyway gives an output that depends on timing and is never reproducible. Failing before any build runs names the cycle so the user can break it.

cases.title: A project listing itself as a dependency is no cycle: `^build` runs its build
cases.why: A package cannot be its own dependency, so a self entry in its manifest orders nothing. Treating it as a cycle fails a run that has a clear and valid order. The right reading ignores the self edge and runs the build once. A package that lists itself is a common slip in a manifest, and it should not block every build of that package.

cases.title: At a concurrency of 1, independent tasks run one at a time
cases.why: A concurrency of 1 is how a user says tasks must not overlap, often because they share a port, a database or a lock file. Running two at once anyway breaks that promise and gives failures that come and go with timing. The limit has to hold exactly, not on average.

cases.title: At a concurrency of 2, no more than two tasks run at once
cases.why: The concurrency limit caps how many tasks run at once, so a run fits the machine’s memory and cores. Going over it can run a CI machine out of memory or slow every task down. The cap must hold at every moment, including when one task ends and the next ones start.

cases.title: Tasks that fail still count against the concurrency limit while they run
cases.why: A failing task is still a process using its slot until it exits. Freeing the slot when the failure is first noticed, or starting the next task early, lets more tasks run than the limit allows. The limit exists for the shared resources, and those are still in use until the process is gone.

cases.title: A concurrency far above the number of tasks runs them all and ends
cases.why: A concurrency higher than the number of tasks simply means no limit in practice. Every task should run and the run should end normally. Hanging while waiting for work that will never come, or refusing the setting, breaks a common choice such as a large fixed value in CI.

cases.title: A failure at the bottom of a chain runs nothing above it
cases.why: When a dependency fails, everything that builds on it would read a missing or broken output. Running lib and app anyway wastes time and can produce output that looks fine but is built on nothing. Skipping them keeps the failure in one place, where the user can see its real cause.

cases.why: When nothing a task reads has changed, its last result is still right, so replaying it is safe. Running it again spends CI minutes and local time on work whose answer is already known. Across a monorepo of many tasks, this is what lets a run with no changes finish in seconds instead of taking the full build time.

cases.title: Editing an input runs the task again
cases.why: A changed input means the stored result was computed from source that no longer exists. Replaying it would ship output built from the old code under a green run. Seeing every edit to a declared input is the most basic promise a cache makes, and every other saving depends on it.

cases.title: A same-size edit right after a commit runs the task again
cases.why: Change detection must rest on content, not on size and timestamps alone. An edit that keeps the file’s length and lands in the same second as a commit can look untouched to a check based on file stats. A tool that trusts such a check replays the old output, and the edit never reaches the build.

cases.title: A new file under an input glob runs the task again
cases.why: A glob names a set of files, and adding a file changes that set. A build that concatenates, bundles or tests everything under `src/` gives different output once a new file exists. Keying only on the files seen before would replay a bundle that is missing the new module.

cases.title: Deleting an input runs the task again
cases.why: Removing a file changes the input set just as editing one does. A task that bundles a directory must stop including the deleted file. Replaying the old result would ship code that is gone from the tree, such as a removed module or a test that should no longer run.

cases.title: Renaming an input runs the task again
cases.why: A file’s path is part of what a task reads, not only its bytes. A rename can change order, module names or import paths, so the output can differ even when no content changed. A key built only from the set of content hashes sees the same bytes and replays output that still names the old file.

cases.title: An edit deep in a nested input directory runs the task again
cases.why: A recursive glob covers every depth, and a change at any depth counts. A tool that stops walking early, or trusts a directory’s own timestamp, can miss an edit several levels down. Real sources nest deeply, so missing such an edit replays stale output for ordinary work.

cases.title: An edit to an input named with spaces, `$` and quotes runs the task again
cases.why: File names with spaces, quotes or `$` are legal and occur in real repos, for example among assets and fixtures. If such a name is mangled when it is listed, quoted or passed through a shell, the file drops out of the key. Edits to it then never rerun the task, and the build ships its old content.

cases.title: An edit to an input with a non-ASCII name runs the task again
cases.why: Non-ASCII file names are ordinary on every current file system and must map to the same path every time. git escapes such names in its plain output; a reader that does not undo the escaping loses the file from the key. Edits to it then replay the old output.

cases.title: Undoing an edit replays the first run’s outputs, not the edited ones
cases.why: A key must depend only on the current inputs, so going back to old inputs must give back the old outputs. After an undo, the tree must hold what the first run produced, not the edited run’s output. A tool that keeps whatever it wrote last leaves output from code that is no longer in the tree, under a green run.

cases.title: A file outside the task’s inputs changes nothing
cases.why: Declared inputs are the contract: only those files can change the result. Rerunning a build because a README or another unrelated file changed wastes time on every docs edit. Explicit inputs are what let a cache stay warm across changes that cannot matter to the task.

cases.title: A file a `!` input pattern takes back changes nothing
cases.why: A `!` pattern is the user stating that a file does not affect the task. Notes, another tool’s fixtures or generated docs often sit inside a source folder. Ignoring the exclusion reruns the task on edits the user has said cannot change its output, and the cache loses its value for that folder.

cases.title: A gitignored file under an input glob changes nothing
cases.why: Files git ignores are local state such as logs, editor files and caches, not part of the source. They differ between machines and change on their own. Keying on them gives every machine a different key, so the cache misses on every CI runner and laptop even when the committed source is identical.

cases.title: A build that writes a fresh committed source map every run is replayed when nothing changed
cases.why: Many repos commit their build output, and some builds stamp it, like a source map with a build id. Keyed by the bytes on disk, each run’s own rewrite changes the next run’s key, so the build never replays though no source changed. Keyed by the version git holds, the second run is a replay, and an edit the user commits still moves the key.

cases.title: A task with caching off runs on every run
cases.why: Turning caching off is an explicit request to run the command every time. Such tasks often have effects beyond their outputs, such as a deploy, a migration or a fetch of fresh data. Replaying one would skip that effect while reporting success. The cost of running again is the price the user chose.

cases.title: Changing a task’s command runs it again
cases.why: The command produces the output as much as the source files do, so it is part of the key. Changing a flag or a script line and getting the old result back makes the edit look like it did nothing. A developer then debugs a config that is already right while the cache serves output from the old one.

cases.title: Changing a dependency’s command rebuilds the projects that read its output
cases.why: A dependency’s new command produces new output, and projects built from that output must rebuild. If only the dependency reruns, its dependants keep the output they built from its previous result. The tree then holds a library built one way and an app built against the other, under a green run.

cases.title: Declaring a new output runs the task again so the cache holds it
cases.why: An entry saved before an output was declared does not hold that output, so it cannot be replayed as if it did. A hit here would restore a tree without the newly declared files, and anything that reads them fails or reads leftovers. Running once more stores the full set of outputs for later hits.

cases.title: Committing a change keeps the entry the uncommitted run saved
cases.why: A cache entry belongs to the content a task reads, not to whether that content is committed. Running a build and then committing the same files changes nothing the task reads. Missing here would make every commit pay again for work done minutes before, which is most of the time a developer spends waiting.

cases.title: An edit that keeps a source’s length, right after a run, runs the task again
cases.why: A cache key must come from a file’s bytes, not its size or timestamp. An edit that keeps the length, right after a run, can leave both the size and a coarse mtime unchanged. A runner that trusts them replays the old output, and the developer tests or ships a build that does not match the source.

cases.title: Writing a source again with the same bytes replays the task
cases.why: A key built from content does not change when a file is written again with the same bytes. Formatters, branch switches and code generators often touch files without changing them. If a moved mtime alone reran the task, the cache would miss after every checkout or save, and CI would redo work whose result is already stored.

cases.title: Adding an empty file under the inputs runs the task again
cases.why: Which files exist under the inputs is input too, even when a file is empty. A command such as `ls`, a bundler’s glob or a test runner looking for test files reads the list of names. If an empty file changed no key, the runner would replay output that misses the new file, and nothing would warn.

cases.title: Changing one byte in the middle of a binary input runs the task again
cases.why: Inputs are bytes, and a binary file must be hashed as bytes. A runner that reads it as text, stops at a zero byte or normalises its encoding can see two different files as one. A changed image, font or compiled asset would then replay the old output, and the shipped build would carry the old file.

cases.title: Changing the last byte of a 2 MB input runs the task again
cases.why: A key must cover the whole of every input, not a prefix or a sample. Hashing only the start of a large file is cheaper, but a change at its end, such as an appended record or a data table’s last row, goes unseen. The runner replays output built from the old file, and the change never reaches the build.

cases.title: A declared variable set to its own name is not the same as the variable unset
cases.why: A declared variable’s key must tell an unset variable apart from every value it can take. A key that writes the name in place of a missing value makes `MODE=MODE` and no `MODE` look the same. The second run then replays `unset` where the command should print `MODE`. Name and value must be encoded so that no value can stand in for absence.

cases.title: A task reading every project file replays though a sibling task wrote its gitignored output: ignored in the workspace’s .gitignore
cases.why: A gitignored file is local state, not source, so it is not an input even of a task that reads every project file. Here the build writes `dist`, ignored in the workspace’s .gitignore. Git does not list it, and a runner that hashes it anyway reruns the reader after every build, so the test never replays. Ignores count wherever git reads them.

cases.title: A same-size edit right after a commit runs the task again
cases.why: Right after a commit, git cannot always tell a same-size edit from its stat, since both can fall in the same second (racy git). A runner that trusts git’s index there keys the new bytes as the committed blob, and replays the old build. The bytes on disk must be read whenever the stat cannot prove them unchanged.

cases.title: Staging and committing a deleted input replays what the run after the deletion stored
cases.why: Deleting a file, then staging and committing the deletion, leaves the same files on disk at each step. The run after the deletion stored a result for that tree. A runner that keys on git’s state, not the files, misses at each git step and rebuilds the same tree, which costs CI time on every pull request that deletes a file.

cases.title: A file added with `git add -N` keys its bytes: an edit to it runs the task again

A runner that trusts the index for the file keys every version of it as empty, so edits replay the old build. Such a file must be hashed from disk, like an untracked one.

A runner that drops or rewrites them sends the task’s temp files where the host never pointed it, filling a small disk or sharing files between jobs. cases.title: A task that exits non-zero fails the run
cases.why: A non-zero exit is how a command says it failed, and the run’s exit code is what CI and scripts read. A runner that reports success over a failed task lets a broken build merge and deploy. The task’s own output is shown so the developer can see what failed without running it again.

cases.title: A failed task is not replayed as a success next time
cases.why: Only a successful run is a result worth keeping. A stored failure would replay the same error without trying again, so a flaky test or a fixed environment could never pass. A failure saved as a pass would be worse: a broken build hidden behind a green run. So a failed task runs again every time.

cases.title: A failed dependency stops the projects that need it from running
cases.why: A task that depends on another reads what that one produced. If the dependency failed, its output is missing or half written, and a dependant built on it either fails with a confusing second error or passes on stale files. Skipping the dependants keeps the first real error in front of the developer and saves the time spent building on a broken base.

cases.title: Fixing a failed task’s input makes the next run pass and build
cases.why: A fix to an input is a new input, so the task must run again on it and succeed. A runner that remembered the failure by task name, not by input, would keep failing after the fix and push the user to wipe the cache. The output on disk is the one the passing run wrote.

cases.title: A task killed by a signal fails the run and is not cached
cases.why: A task killed by a signal never finished, so whatever it wrote is partial. Treating the death as success, or caching it, would replay half-written output as a green result on every later run. The run fails so CI sees it, and the next run tries the task again from scratch.

cases.title: A task that writes to stderr and exits 0 succeeds
cases.why: Many tools print warnings, progress and deprecation notes to stderr while succeeding. The exit code is the only contract a command makes about failure. A runner that failed on stderr output would break builds over harmless warnings and push users to silence useful diagnostics.

cases.title: Asking for a task no project declares fails the run
cases.why: A task name no project declares is almost always a typo or a stale script. If the run exits 0 having run nothing, CI reports green while no test or build ran at all. Failing loudly turns the typo into a message the developer sees at once, instead of a gap found weeks later.

cases.title: Tasks that depend on each other in a cycle fail the run before any runs
cases.why: A cycle has no valid order: each task waits on the other, so neither can correctly go first. Starting one anyway means it runs without the input it declared it needs. Refusing before anything runs points at the config mistake, rather than leaving a half-run graph or a run that waits forever.

cases.title: Asked to fail fast, a run stops its running tasks at the first failure
cases.why: Failing fast means the first error ends the run now: the developer or the CI job learns of it at once instead of waiting for every other task already started. A run that lets those tasks finish costs the whole wait it was asked to skip, and a task cut short must leave no output behind as if it had finished.

cases.title: A forced run runs every task past its cache entry, and the next run replays what it saved
cases.why: Forcing a run asks for every task to run regardless of what the cache holds, often because the user suspects an entry. The fresh results must then replace the saved ones. A force that saves nothing leaves the doubted entry in place for the next run to replay.

vite-task.detail: `--cache` and `--no-cache` turn caching on or off; no run ignores entries and saves fresh ones.

nix.detail: A valid output is never built again: `--check` rebuilds to compare and saves nothing.

cases.title: A forced run that fails leaves the stored pass for the same inputs, and a read-only run replays it
cases.why: A forced run can fail for a reason outside the task’s inputs: a flaky network, a full disk. The entry an earlier run saved for those same inputs is still right. A runner that lets the failure poison it rebuilds on every later run, and a read-only run, which cannot save the fix, never hits again.

nx.detail: Nx has no run that reads the cache and writes nothing to it.

vite-task.detail: `--cache` and `--no-cache` turn caching on or off; no run ignores entries and saves fresh ones. No run reads the cache and writes nothing to it.

cases.title: A run that only reads the cache replays a hit, and saves nothing for a miss
cases.why: A read-only cache lets a run use what others built without writing, as an untrusted branch build should. A hit must still replay, or the mode saves nothing. A miss must run and leave the cache as it was, so the next normal run builds it again instead of replaying it.

vite-task.detail: No run reads the cache and writes nothing to it.

nix.detail: Building writes the store: no build reads it without writing.

cases.title: A planned run runs no task, writes no output, and saves nothing
cases.why: A planned run shows what would run without running it. No command may start, no output may be written and no cache entry may be saved. A plan that runs tasks surprises the user with side effects, and one that saves entries can later replay results nothing ever built.

nx.detail: Nx has no run that plans and runs nothing.

vite-task.detail: Vite Task has no run that plans and runs nothing.

cases.title: A variable passed through reaches the task
cases.why: A pass-through variable is one the task needs to run, such as a token or a path, but whose value does not change the output. It must reach the command, or the task fails or behaves differently. Keeping it out of the key is a choice about caching, not about whether the task sees it.

nix.detail: A variable reaches a build only as an attribute, which keys it.

cases.title: A change to a variable passed through, not keyed, replays the task
cases.why: The user declared that this variable reaches the task but does not change its output, such as a log level or a token. Changing it therefore leaves the result as it was. Running the task again ignores that declaration and costs a full build on every machine where the value differs.

nix.detail: A variable reaches a build only as an attribute, which keys it.

cases.title: A task ordered after a dependency, but not keyed on it, replays when only the dependency changes
cases.why: The task was told to run after its dependency but not to key on it, because it never reads what the dependency produces. A change only in the dependency leaves this task’s inputs as they were. Running it again ignores that declaration and costs a build that gives the same bytes.

turbo.detail: A dependency’s hash always keys its dependants: no task orders a dependency without it.

nix.detail: A dependency’s output path is its dependant’s input: it always keys it.

cases.title: A linked git worktree of the same commit replays what the main checkout built
cases.why: A linked git worktree at the same commit holds the same files as the main checkout. The task’s inputs are identical, so the result already built is right here too. Building again because the path differs makes every extra worktree start cold, which is the cost a shared cache should remove.

cases.title: A run started through a link to the workspace replays what the real path built
cases.why: Opening the workspace through a link leaves every file and the commit the same; only the path the shell shows differs. The task’s inputs are identical, so the saved result is right. Building again because of the path makes the same tree cost twice depending on how the user reached it.

cases.title: A task that exits 0 but never writes a declared output fails, and nothing is cached
cases.why: A declared output that matches no file after the command means the build did not do its job: the output path is wrong, or the tool skipped its emit. Treated as a success, the empty result is cached and every later run reports a hit that restores nothing. Failing the task says so where CI shows it, and the next run tries again.

cases.why: Some outputs exist only some of the time, like a coverage report a test run writes only when asked. Marking such an output optional keeps the strict check on every other output while this one may be absent. The run passes, the outputs that were written are cached, and the next run replays them.

cases.title: Two tasks that share one resource never run at the same time
cases.why: Tasks that share one port, one database or one emulator break each other when they overlap, and the break comes and goes with timing. Lowering the whole run to one task at a time fixes it at the cost of every other task. Naming the shared resource on those tasks keeps them apart while everything else still runs in parallel.

cases.title: A task that prints nothing past its idle limit is killed and fails the run
cases.why: A hung test often stops printing long before any wall-clock limit would end it, and that limit has to be generous enough for the slowest healthy run. A limit on silence ends the hung task early while a long task that keeps reporting progress runs on. The run fails, so CI shows the hang instead of waiting out its own timeout.

cases.title: A task that keeps printing outlives its idle limit and succeeds
cases.why: An idle limit measures silence, not length. A task that runs longer than the limit but prints along the way is working and must succeed. A runner that read the limit as a wall-clock one would kill healthy long builds.

cases.why: A pinned checksum says exactly which bytes a task must produce, as a downloaded toolchain or a vendored archive should. A build that writes anything else is wrong, however it exits, and caching it would spread the wrong bytes. Once the bytes match, the task passes.

cases.title: A check run rebuilds a cached task and fails when its bytes come out different
cases.why: A cache is only as good as the tasks it stores: one whose output changes from run to run makes every hit a guess about which build you got. A check run rebuilds the cached task and compares, so the nondeterminism shows up as a failure in one place. Without it, it shows up as builds that differ by machine.

cases.why: A check run is meant to prove a cached result, and a reproducible task must pass it. A check that failed reproducible tasks too, by comparing timestamps or paths, would be switched off and catch nothing.

cases.title: A task that needs a server starts only once the server accepts connections on its port
cases.why: Many servers print nothing reliable when they are ready, but every one of them opens its port. Waiting for the port means a dependant never meets a closed socket, whatever the server logs. Starting the dependant as soon as the process spawns gives e2e failures that come and go with machine speed.

cases.title: A run reports that a task missed the cache
cases.why: Knowing which tasks missed the cache is how a user finds what broke caching. A key that changes on every run looks like a slow build until the report shows the miss. Without it, a team cannot tell a cold cache from one that never hits, and cannot find the input that keeps changing.

cases.title: A run reports that a task was replayed
cases.why: A report of each hit tells the user what was replayed rather than run. When a result looks wrong, the first question is whether the task ran at all. It is also how a team checks that CI gets the reuse it expects, and notices when a change quietly turns hits into misses.

cases.title: A run reports how long each task took
cases.why: Per-task time is the number a build is tuned with. Without it, a user cannot find the slow task on the critical path or tell whether a change made a task slower. The total time of a run alone hides which task to fix, since many tasks run at once and overlap.

vite-task.detail: `vp run --last-details` names the time a hit saved, never how long a task took in this run.

nix.detail: nix-build lists the derivations it builds, never how long one took.

cases.title: A run reports how long a replay took, not the original run
cases.why: A replay’s time is the time to restore it, not the original command’s time. Reporting the original time makes a hit look as slow as a miss and hides whether the cache helps at all. It also hides a slow restore, such as a large artifact from a slow store. The original time belongs to the run that paid it.

vite-task.detail: `vp run --last-details` names the time a hit saved, never how long a task took in this run.

nix.detail: nix-build lists the derivations it builds, never how long one took.

cases.title: A run reports each task’s CPU time
cases.why: CPU time shows how much work a task does, apart from how long it waited. A task that waits on the network and one that compiles for the same span look alike by wall time. CPU time tells a user which tasks gain from more cores and which from less waiting, and whether parallel runs are starved.

cases.title: A run reports each task’s peak memory
cases.why: Peak memory decides how many tasks fit on a machine at once. Without it, a user sizing CI runners or a concurrency limit guesses, and a run can be killed for running out of memory with no hint of which task caused it. Per-task numbers show which task needs the larger machine.

cases.why: The size of what a task writes is what the cache must store and move. Large outputs make saves and restores slow and fill a remote cache. Reporting it per task shows which outputs to trim, split or leave uncached, instead of guessing from the size of the whole cache.

cases.why: On a replay, the bytes restored are the cost of the hit. A hit that pulls a large artifact over the network can take longer than running the task. Reporting the restored size lets a user see when that happens and narrow what the task declares as output.

cases.title: Two tasks with no edge between them run at the same time
cases.why: Tasks with no dependency between them can run side by side, and a run that has cores to spare should use them. Here each task waits a while for the other to start, so run one after the other they each wait out the full delay. Running independent work in turn makes a monorepo’s wall time the sum of its tasks instead of its longest path.

cases.title: A task that closes its output and keeps working is waited for until it exits
cases.why: A process can close its output streams and go on working, as a daemonizing tool or a quiet build step does. The task ends when its process exits, not when its output ends. A runner that takes the closed stream as the end starts the dependant on a half-written output, or ends the run with the task still running behind it.

cases.title: Putting back the outputs a task first declared replays the entry saved for them
cases.why: An entry is saved under the task’s config as it was, so going back to that config finds it again. A team that tries a wider output set and reverts it should get its old hits back, not rebuild. The entry still holds every output the restored config names, so replaying it leaves the right tree.

cases.title: Switching a declared variable back and forth replays each value’s own result
cases.why: Each value of a keyed variable has its own entry, and a new value must not push out the old one. Builds that switch between modes, such as dev and prod or two targets, go back and forth all day. A cache that keeps only the latest value rebuilds on every switch, though both results are already known.

cases.title: Running a task with one set of args, then another, then each again replays both
cases.why: Forwarded args are part of the key, so each set of args has its own entry. Running tests for one file, then another, then the first again is ordinary work. A cache that keeps only the last args reruns work whose result it already had, while keeping both costs nothing in correctness.

cases.title: A project whose package.json does not parse fails the run
cases.why: A manifest that does not parse leaves the project’s name, dependencies and tasks unknown. Skipping the project lets the run go green with its tasks never run and its dependants built in the wrong order. Failing at once names the broken file while the mistake is fresh.

cases.title: Replaying an older build over a tree holding the same directory link restores through it
cases.why: A store layout such as `dist/pkg -> store/pkg` is common in package builds, and the link is already there when an older entry is replayed. The restore must put the old files back and leave the link as a link to the same directory. A restore that trips over the existing link fails a run that should replay, and one that follows or flattens it leaves the newer build’s bytes or a copy where a link belongs.

cases.title: Forwarded args such as `--help`, `--version` and `-v` reach the task, not the runner
cases.why: Args after the task belong to the task’s command, whatever they look like. `--help`, `--version` and `-v` are also flags of every runner, and a runner that reads them itself prints its own help or version and runs nothing, often with exit 0. The user asked the task for its help or a verbose run and got neither, with a green exit hiding it.

cases.title: A dependency reached by `^build` and by `b#build` builds once, first
cases.why: Naming one task twice, once through the package graph and once by its full name, asks for the same work twice. It must run once and finish before the task that needs it. Two runs of it waste time and can rewrite its output while the dependant reads it; dropping either edge can start the dependant early.

cases.title: Explicit `project#task` edges chain: each one’s own edges run first, and nothing else
cases.why: An explicit edge names a task, and that task brings its own dependsOn with it. deploy needs utils#lint, which needs core#build and utils#build, so all of them run first, in that order. A runner that follows only the first hop lints against a core that was never built; one that pulls in core#clean or the tests runs work nobody named.

cases.title: A negation with a trailing slash, `!src/gen/`, takes that directory’s tree out of the key
cases.why: A trailing slash only says the path is a directory: `!src/gen/` takes back every file under it, as `src/` keys every file under src. Read as a bare pattern, it matches nothing and the generated files stay in the key. Each regeneration then reruns a task the user excluded them from, while edits outside it must still rerun.

cases.title: A command of multi-byte characters runs byte-exact, and changing its last character runs it again
cases.why: A command is text of any script, and `echo ああ` must print exactly that. A runner that counts characters as bytes cuts the command inside a character or drops its tail, so the shell runs something else, or two commands differing only at the end share one key. The edit then replays the old output under a green run.

cases.title: A forwarded arg of multi-byte characters reaches the command byte-exact and keys the task
cases.why: Args forwarded to a task are its input as much as its files are. An emoji must reach the command as the same bytes the user typed, and a different emoji is a different run. A runner that mangles or truncates the arg feeds the command something else, or replays the result of one arg for another.

cases.title: Two excludes alone each take their project out of every project
cases.why: An exclude given with no include takes from the whole workspace, and a second exclude takes from that same set. A runner that lets the second exclude replace the first, or reads it as an include, runs a project the user ruled out. That can be the slow or broken project the excludes were there to skip.

cases.title: An exclude alone that names no project runs every project, or refuses
cases.why: Excluding a project that does not exist leaves the whole workspace: nothing was taken out. Refusing the run as a likely typo is also fair, before anything starts. Running nothing and exiting 0 is not: CI goes green having checked no project at all.

cases.title: The three tasks one task releases run at the same time, and the task over them reads all three
cases.why: When a shared dependency finishes, every task waiting only on it is ready at that moment and can start together. Here each of the three waits a while for the other two to start, so run one at a time they each wait out the full delay. A runner that releases ready tasks one by one turns a wide graph into a chain, and the wall time becomes the sum of the branches instead of the longest one.

cases.title: Either of a dependency’s two output trees, deleted alone, is back before a rebuilding dependant reads it
cases.why: A task that writes two trees, as a build writing `dist` and `types` does, is only present when both are. Deleting one and keeping the other is what a partial clean or a tool that prunes one directory leaves. A runner that sees one tree on disk and calls the dependency done lets the dependant build against a missing file, and fail or ship without it.

cases.title: A `!**/*.bak` input still keys a file named plain `bak`
cases.why: An exclusion by suffix means files ending in `.bak`, not every name holding those letters. A file named plain `bak`, with no dot, is a source like any other, and the user never took it back. A tool that matches the suffix loosely replays a stale result when that file changes, under a green run.

cases.title: A task closed off from the machine cannot read a system file
cases.why: A file of the machine, such as one under /etc, is an input no key holds and no other machine shares. A build that reads it can give different bytes on two machines under one key. A task closed off from the machine must fail that read, so the build depends only on what it declared.

cases.why: Chaining steps with `&&` is how a task says “only if the previous step passed”. A tool that splits the chain into steps of its own, or runs it through a shell that ignores the status, writes the output of a build whose first step failed. The run must fail and leave nothing the later steps would have written.

cases.title: A command of steps joined by `;` runs each one in order
cases.why: A `;` list runs every step whatever the one before returned, and in the order written. A tool that keeps only the first step, or reorders them, leaves a different file than the same line typed in a terminal. The output must hold both lines, first then second.

cases.title: A `;` list whose first step fails and last step passes succeeds, as the shell says
cases.why: In `sh`, the status of a `;` list is the status of its last command. A tool that fails the task on an earlier step’s status runs something other than the command the user wrote, and a task meant to tolerate a failing probe can never pass. The run succeeds and the last step’s file is there.

cases.title: A command that pipes one program into another writes what the pipe produced
cases.why: Pipes are the most common shell idiom in a task: a generator into a formatter, a list into a filter. A tool that does not run the command through a shell passes `|` as an argument to the first program. The output holds the transformed text.

cases.title: A pipeline whose first program fails and last program passes succeeds, as `sh` says
cases.why: A plain `sh` pipeline returns the status of its last program; only `set -o pipefail` changes that, and the user did not write it. A tool that runs commands with pipefail on, or under another shell, fails a task the user’s own terminal passes. The run succeeds.

cases.title: A command `false || …` runs the fallback and succeeds
cases.why: An `||` fallback is how a task tolerates a step that may fail: a cache warmer, an optional tool. The status of the list is the fallback’s. A tool that fails the task on the first step’s status breaks every such command. The fallback’s file is there and the run succeeds.

cases.title: A command redirecting its error stream into a file writes it there
cases.why: A task that captures a tool’s diagnostics with `2>` relies on the shell to open the file. A tool that runs the command without a shell, or captures stderr itself before the redirect applies, leaves the file empty. The file holds what the command wrote to its error stream.

cases.title: A variable set in front of a program, `FOO=bar prog`, reaches that program
cases.why: Setting a variable for one program is plain shell (`NODE_ENV=production vite build`). A tool that splits the command on spaces runs a program named `FOO=bar`. The program sees the value the command gave it.

cases.title: A command substitution, `$(…)`, is replaced by what it printed
cases.why: Tasks compute values inline: `--version=$(git describe)`, `$(cat VERSION)`. The shell runs the inner command and splices its output in. A tool that passes the text through unexpanded writes `$(cat src/a.txt)` into the output. The output holds the expanded text.

cases.title: A backtick substitution is replaced by what it printed
cases.why: Backticks are the older spelling of `$(…)` and still common in scripts copied into configs. The shell runs the inner command and splices its output in. A tool that treats backticks as text writes them into the output. The output holds the expanded text.

cases.title: A `cd` inside parentheses does not move the rest of the command
cases.why: A subshell runs its steps in a child shell: `(cd sub && make)` leaves the outer command where it was. A tool that runs each step of the command in turn in one process, or strips the parentheses, writes the output into the wrong directory. The output lands in the project’s dist.

cases.title: A command written over several lines runs every line, in order
cases.why: A long task is often written one step per line. In `sh`, a newline ends a command like `;` does. A tool that keeps only the first line, or joins the lines into one argument list, runs part of the task and passes. The output holds every line’s write.

cases.title: A here-document in a command writes the lines it holds
cases.why: A here-document is how a command writes a small file inline: a config, a banner. The shell reads the lines up to the marker as the program’s input. A tool that runs the first line alone leaves the shell waiting for input or writes nothing. The file holds the document’s lines.

cases.title: A glob inside single quotes reaches the program as text, not as file names
cases.why: Quoting is how a command passes a pattern to a program that expands it itself (`eslint 'src/**/*.ts'`). The shell must not expand a quoted glob. A tool that strips quotes or expands it anyway hands the program a list of files it did not ask for. The program sees the pattern.

cases.title: An unquoted glob in a command expands to the matching files, sorted
cases.why: An unquoted glob is the shell’s to expand, in sorted order, before the program runs. A tool that passes the pattern through hands the program a file named `src/*.txt`. The program sees each matching name.

cases.title: A `$NAME` inside single quotes reaches the program as text
cases.why: Single quotes keep everything literal: a regex with `$`, a template with `${name}`. A tool that expands variables in the command itself before the shell sees it rewrites what the user wrote. The program sees the dollar sign and the name.

cases.title: Text in braces such as `{projectRoot}` reaches the shell as written, never filled in by the tool
cases.why: A command is the user’s shell line, run as written. A tool that fills in its own placeholders inside it changes what runs: a JSON literal, a brace expansion or a template a program reads can hold the same words. The program sees the braces and the word.

cases.title: A command whose last output has no newline still succeeds and writes its file
cases.why: Plenty of programs end their output without a newline (`printf`). The tool must pass the bytes through and not wait for a line that never ends. A tool that waits hangs the run, and one that appends a newline changes the file. The file holds exactly what was written.

cases.title: A task’s command runs in its project’s directory
cases.why: Every relative path in a command (`src/`, `dist/`, `tsconfig.json`) means the project’s own. A tool that runs commands from the workspace root reads and writes another tree. The command sees its project’s directory as the current one.

cases.title: Run from a subdirectory of the project, the command still runs in the project’s directory
cases.why: Where the user stands decides what is selected, not where the command runs. A tool that starts the command in the user’s current directory makes every relative path in it point somewhere else depending on where the run was typed. The command sees its project’s directory.

cases.title: The workspace-root project’s task runs in the workspace root
cases.why: A root task (a repo-wide lint, a docs build) works on the whole tree from the root. A tool that runs it in some member, or in a scratch directory, reads the wrong files. The command reads the root’s own `src/r.txt`, which only the root holds.

cases.title: Clearing the executable bit of a committed input runs the task again
cases.why: A task can read a file’s mode (a packager that keeps the bit, a check that a script is runnable). Taking the bit away is as much a change as adding it. A tool that keys only content, or only notices the bit being set, replays the result built from the executable file. The output says the file is plain.

cases.title: Committing an input made executable replays the build of the executable file
cases.why: A commit records what is already on disk; the file is the same before and after. A tool that keys the working tree for a dirty file and git’s record for a clean one must give both the same value. Otherwise every commit costs a rebuild of work already done. The run after the commit replays.

cases.title: Making a root input executable runs the task that names it again
cases.why: A shared script at the root (`scripts/build.sh`) is often named by every project’s task. Its mode is part of what the task reads, as for a project file. A tool that keys root files by content alone replays a build made while the script could not run. The second run runs and sees the script executable.

cases.title: A run of one project replays what a run of every project stored, with an untracked input
cases.why: A tool may look for untracked files only under the projects a run selects. Whatever it scans, the same file must key the task the same way. A selected run that keys an untracked file differently misses an entry the full run just saved, and every CI job that selects a project rebuilds it. The selected run replays.

cases.title: Selecting a project nested in another, an edit to its untracked file runs its task again
cases.why: A project inside another project’s directory owns its own files, untracked ones too. A tool that scans untracked files only at the selected projects’ top level, or hands the nested project’s files to its parent, misses the edit and replays a stale build. The nested project’s task runs again with the new content.

cases.title: A run of one project ignores a file its own `.gitignore` ignores, as a full run does
cases.why: Git’s ignore rules come from every `.gitignore` between the root and the file. A tool that scans only the selected project may read the project’s rules but miss the root’s, or the other way round, and key a scratch file the full run ignores. Rebuilding on a scratch file wastes the run. An edit to the ignored file replays; an edit to a kept one runs.

cases.title: Excluding the workspace-root project by name leaves out its task and keeps the members’
cases.why: The root project is a project like any other, and an exclude by its name takes it out. A tool that cannot name the root runs its task anyway, or treats the exclude as excluding every member under the root’s directory. The members’ tasks run and the root’s does not.

cases.title: A task that lists, removes and remakes its output folder replays on the next run
cases.why: Build tools clean their output folder before writing a new one: they look at it, delete it, make it again and check it. None of that reads an input. A tool that counts the task’s own folder as something it read sees it change every run and never replays. The second run replays and the folder comes back.

cases.title: An output edited by hand after a clean-and-rebuild task is put back on the next run
cases.why: Deleting its output folder does not make that folder an input of the task. An edit to the output afterwards is a damaged result, not new input: the next run must leave the bytes the task produces. Keeping the hand edit leaves a tree no build made. The file holds the task’s content again.

cases.title: A task that writes a temporary folder and renames it to its output caches and restores the output
cases.why: Vite’s dependency optimizer writes `deps_temp_*` and renames it to `deps` so readers never see a half-written folder. The output is the renamed folder, written by a rename rather than by file writes. A tool that tracks what the task wrote file by file can miss it. The second run replays, and the folder comes back after it is deleted.

cases.title: A task that lists the project folder holding its output replays on the next run
cases.why: A code generator often lists the folder it writes into. Its own output appears in that listing after the first run. A tool that keys what the task listed sees a new entry and reruns every time, so the task never replays. The second run replays.

cases.title: A task that checks its own output folder after writing replays on the next run
cases.why: A build tool checks that its output folder exists once it has written it. The folder is the task’s own output, made by this run. A tool that counts every path the task looked at as an input sees the folder’s times change and reruns every time. The second run replays.

cases.title: An output link to a committed file outside the outputs comes back as the same link
cases.why: A build can link a source file into its output rather than copy it, as pnpm does for packages. The link is the output; the file it points at belongs to the source tree. A cache that stores the target’s bytes in place of the link, or drops the link, restores a different tree. The link comes back pointing where it did.

cases.title: An input naming the file a task writes into its output directory does not rerun the task
cases.why: Input and output patterns often overlap: `**/*.txt` in, `out/**` out, with `out` not ignored by git. The files the task wrote are its result, not something it read. A tool that keys its own output reruns the task every time, and caching it is pointless. The second run replays, and an edit to a real source still runs it; refusing such a pair before any task runs is fine too.

cases.title: Two inputs that swap their contents run the task again
cases.why: Each file’s content belongs to its path. Swapping two files leaves the same set of contents under other names, and the task’s result can differ (`a` imports `b`, not the reverse). A key over the contents without their paths, or one that sorts them, sees nothing change and replays the old result. The task runs and writes the swapped pairing.

cases.title: Renaming an input to differ only in case runs the task again
cases.why: On a case-sensitive filesystem `Readme.md` and `README.md` are different files, and a task that lists or imports by name sees a different tree. A tool that folds case in its key, as it might to match a Mac, replays the build of the old name. The task runs and lists the new name.

cases.title: Renaming a directory under the inputs, its files unchanged, runs the task again
cases.why: A directory’s name is part of every path under it: a route, a module path, a package entry. Moving `src/v1` to `src/v2` keeps every file’s bytes and changes what the task produces. A key over file contents without full paths replays the old build. The task runs and writes the new path.

cases.title: An input file replaced by a link to a file with other content runs the task again
cases.why: A task reading through a link reads the target’s bytes. Swapping a file for a link (a shared config linked in, a vendored file deduplicated) changes what the task reads even though the path stays. A tool that keys the link’s own entry, or skips links, replays the build of the old file. The task runs and writes the target’s content.

cases.title: An input link replaced by a plain file with other content runs the task again
cases.why: Undoing a link (vendoring a file that was shared) puts new bytes at the same path. A tool that remembers the path as a link and keys its target string, or the target file, misses that the content now lives in the file itself. The task runs and writes the file’s content.

cases.title: An edit made through a hard link outside the inputs reruns the task reading the other name
cases.why: Two hard links are one file: writing through either changes both, and the input’s path never appears in the write. A tool that watches or stats only the paths written, or caches a file’s hash by the path that changed, keeps the input’s old hash and replays a stale build. The task runs and writes the new content.

cases.title: An input deleted and written again with the same bytes replays the task
cases.why: A checkout or a formatter often deletes a file and writes it back unchanged. Its bytes and path are what they were, so the result is too. A tool that keys a file’s inode or times reruns for nothing on every such touch. The run replays.

cases.title: An empty directory created under the inputs replays the task
cases.why: Git does not track directories, and an input glob over files matches no empty one. Creating an empty folder (an editor’s scratch, a tool’s placeholder) changes no file the task reads. A tool that keys directories reruns for nothing. The run replays.

cases.title: An input emptied to zero bytes runs the task again
cases.why: An empty file is a real state: a truncated config, an emptied fixture. A tool that treats an empty file as absent, or skips zero-length files when hashing, keys the same before and after deleting every byte of one, and replays the old result. The task runs and writes nothing from the file.

cases.title: One edited file among two thousand inputs runs the task again
cases.why: A large project’s key covers thousands of files, and tools take shortcuts there: hashing only a sample, trusting a directory’s time, stopping at a size limit. An edit to one file deep in the list must still change the key. The task runs and writes the new content.

cases.title: A variable keying a dependency’s build reaches the dependant that reads its output
cases.why: The dependency writes the variable’s value into its output, and the dependant copies that output. When the value changes, the dependency rebuilds, and so must everything built on what it wrote. A tool that keys the dependant on the dependency’s files but not its variables replays the dependant with the old value inside. The dependant holds the new value.

cases.title: A variable one task declares does not rerun the project’s other task
cases.why: Each task declares what keys it. A `build` keyed on `MODE` beside a `test` that never reads it are two keys. A tool that keys a variable for the whole project reruns every task of it whenever one task’s variable moves. `test` replays.

vite-task.detail: `vp run` runs one task name per run.

cases.title: A variable one project’s task declares does not rerun another project’s task
cases.why: A variable keys the tasks that declare it, wherever the run sets it. A tool that folds every declared variable of the workspace into every task makes an unrelated project rebuild whenever another project’s setting changes. The other project replays.

cases.title: A declared value with a trailing newline is not the same as the value without it
cases.why: A value read from a file (`MODE=$(cat mode)`) keeps or loses its newline depending on how it was set, and a program reading it sees the difference. A tool that trims values before keying replays the result built from the other one. The second run runs and writes the newline.

cases.title: A declared value with a trailing space is not the same as the value without it
cases.why: Spaces are bytes of the value: a path, a flag list, a token. A tool that trims or normalises whitespace before keying replays the result built from the other spelling, though the program sees a different value. The second run runs and writes the space.

cases.title: A declared value of spaces is not the same as an empty value
cases.why: An empty value and one of spaces are different strings, and programs treat them differently (`[ -n "$X" ]`). A tool that trims before keying folds them into one key and replays one’s result for the other. The second run runs.

cases.title: A declared value that changes only in letter case runs the task again
cases.why: Values are case-sensitive: `production` and `Production` are different to every program comparing them. A tool that lowercases values before keying, as it might for names on Windows, replays the other spelling’s result. The second run runs.

cases.title: Declared values that differ only after an `=` or inside quotes key different results
cases.why: Values carry `=` and quotes: a connection string, a JSON blob, `KEY=VAL` pairs. A tool that writes `NAME=VALUE` lines into its key and splits them again at the first `=`, or strips quotes, folds different values into one. The second run runs.

cases.title: A 60 KB declared value reaches the task whole, and a change to its last byte runs it again
cases.why: Variables carry large payloads: a JSON config, a certificate, a list of files. A tool that truncates values in its key, or hashes only a prefix, replays a result built from another value once two values share a long start. The task sees every byte, and the second run runs.

cases.title: A project depending on eight others builds after all eight
cases.why: An app often depends on many libraries at once. The scheduler must hold the app until the last of them finishes, not until the first or until a count of slots frees. A tool that starts the app early reads a library’s output before it exists.

cases.title: Eight projects depending on one library all build after it
cases.why: A shared library sits under many apps. Every app must wait for it, and each must see its finished output. A tool that releases dependants as a batch when the first one is scheduled can start some before the library ends.

cases.title: A chain of twelve projects builds strictly bottom up
cases.why: Deep chains are common in layered monorepos (types, core, sdk, ui, app…). Each link must wait for the one below. A scheduler that walks a fixed number of levels, or orders by name, breaks a long chain in the middle.

cases.title: A three-level tree of projects builds every leaf before its parent and the root last
cases.why: A tree joins pairs of builds at each level. Each parent needs both children, and the root needs everything. A tool that orders by depth alone can still run a parent before a child of the other branch at the same depth finishes.

cases.title: Two chains with nothing between them each keep their own order
cases.why: Unrelated parts of a workspace build side by side. Each chain must stay in order on its own, whatever the other is doing. A scheduler that serialises across chains is slow, and one that loses track of which chain released what breaks an order.

cases.title: Two projects each depending on the same two libraries build after both
cases.why: A W shape (two apps over two shared libraries, each app using both) has every top waiting on every bottom. A tool that pairs dependants with one dependency each, or releases an app when its first library ends, starts it too soon.

cases.title: Three diamonds stacked on each other build in order, each shared node once
cases.why: Stacked diamonds put a shared node at every join, reached by two paths each time. The scheduler must run each join once, after both arms, and only then release the next diamond. Counting paths instead of nodes runs a join twice or early.

cases.title: A project depending on both a library and that library’s dependant builds after both
cases.why: A transitive edge written out (app on core and on ui, ui on core) is redundant but common. It must not change the order: core, then ui, then app. A tool that drops the redundant edge too eagerly, or that releases app when core ends, runs app before ui.

cases.title: A project over one shallow and one deep dependency waits for the deep one
cases.why: Dependencies at different depths finish at different times. The dependant must wait for its slowest path, not for the shortest. A scheduler that orders by depth from the top can start it when the shallow side is done.

cases.title: Six top projects over one shared leaf build the leaf once, first
cases.why: Many apps over one leaf ask for it many times in one run. It runs once, before any of them, and every app sees its one output. A tool that runs it per requester wastes work, and one that releases tops by count starts some early.

cases.title: A ladder of projects, each over the two below it, builds rung by rung
cases.why: A ladder makes every node a join of two paths of different lengths. Each must wait for both. It is the shape where an off-by-one in counting finished dependencies shows: a node released after one of two.

cases.title: Four tasks of one project chained by name run in that order
cases.why: A project’s own pipeline (generate, compile, bundle, pack) is a chain of bare-name edges. Each step must wait for the one before. A tool that treats bare names as hints, or runs a project’s tasks in declaration order, packs before the bundle exists.

cases.title: A task naming two tasks of another project waits for both
cases.why: A task can need two things from one project (its codegen and its build). Both edges are separate: the task waits for each. A tool that keys edges by project, and keeps one task per project, drops the other and starts too soon.

cases.title: A never-cached dependency runs before the cached task that needs it, on every run
cases.why: A never-cached step (a fetch, a codegen from the network) still has dependants. They must wait for it each time it runs, cached or not. A tool that treats an uncached task as outside the graph starts the dependant beside it and reads a half-written file.

cases.title: A failure skips only what depends on it: an unrelated task that starts later still runs
cases.why: A failed library says nothing about an unrelated project. Skipping that project’s work, even work that would only start after the failure, hides every other result of the run and makes the next run rebuild it. The run fails, the failure’s dependant does not run, and the unrelated project still builds.

cases.why: In a diamond the two arms are independent; only the join needs both. A failure in one arm skips the join and nothing else. A tool that cancels the whole subgraph under the shared root throws away the other arm’s result. The other arm runs; the join does not.

cases.title: A failure in the middle of a chain keeps what built below it, and runs nothing above
cases.why: The links below a failure built before it and passed. They stay built and replay next time; the links above never start. A tool that rolls back the whole chain, or starts the links above, leaves a misleading tree. The bottom ran, the top did not.

cases.title: Two failing projects in separate branches each skip only their own dependants
cases.why: A run can hold more than one failure. Each skips what depends on it, and a third branch still builds. A tool that stops at the first failure hides the second, and the user fixes one, reruns, and only then learns of the other. The healthy branch runs.

cases.title: A task whose program does not exist fails, and what depends on it does not run
cases.why: A missing binary (a tool not installed, a typo) makes the shell exit 127. That is a failed task like any other: its dependants must not run on an output that was never written. A tool that treats a spawn error differently from a failing exit can let them start. The run fails and the dependant is skipped.

cases.title: A task running a script without its executable bit fails, and is not cached
cases.why: A script checked in without `+x` cannot run; the shell exits 126. The task failed and nothing it should have written exists. A tool that misreads the spawn error as success, or caches the failure as a pass, replays a build that never happened. The run fails, and fails again next time.

cases.title: A task whose own project’s prerequisite fails does not run, while other projects’ do
cases.why: A `test` that depends on its project’s `lint` must not run when the lint fails. Another project’s test, whose lint passed, has nothing to do with it. A tool that skips by task name across projects skips that one too. The other project’s test runs.

cases.title: A declared value in composed and decomposed Unicode forms keys two results
cases.why: An `é` can be one code point or `e` plus a combining accent: they look alike and are different bytes, and a program comparing them sees two values. A tool that normalises values before keying replays one form’s result for the other. The second run runs.

cases.title: Declared values `1` and `01` key two results
cases.why: Values are strings, not numbers: a version `01`, a port `0080`, a code. A tool that parses numeric-looking values before keying folds them together and replays a result built from the other. The second run runs.

cases.title: A declared value holding a newline is not the same as one holding a space there
cases.why: A tool that writes values one per line into its key, or that normalises whitespace, folds `a b` and `a`+newline+`b` into one key. Programs reading the variable see different values. The second run runs.

cases.title: A run reports a replayed dependency as a hit while its dependant runs
cases.why: When only the app changed, its library replays and the app runs. The report must say so per task, or the user cannot tell whether the library’s cache works. A tool that reports a run as one status, or calls every task of a run with a miss a miss, hides where time went.

cases.title: A run reports the dependant that ran as a miss while its dependency replays
cases.why: The task that actually ran is the one to look at when a run is slow. Its status must be its own, not the first task’s or the run’s. A report that marks every task by the run’s overall cache state points at the wrong task.

cases.title: A forced run reports the task it ran as a miss
cases.why: Forcing a run makes every task run whatever the cache holds. Reporting it as a hit because an entry existed tells the user the task was replayed when it ran. The report says the task missed.

cases.title: A run reports how long a failed task took
cases.why: A task that fails after minutes is the one that wastes CI time. Its duration matters as much as a passing task’s, and more when it times out or flakes. A tool that records time only for successes leaves the slowest failure invisible.

cases.title: A run reports zero bytes for a task that declares no outputs
cases.why: A check (lint, typecheck, test) writes nothing to cache. Its output size is zero, a real value, not a missing one. A tool that reports nothing, or the log’s size, makes cache-size accounting wrong for every check.

cases.title: A change to a variable a dependency passes through replays the dependency and its dependants
cases.why: A passed-through variable (a token, a cache directory) reaches the command without keying it. A tool that still folds it into the dependency’s key cascades the change into every dependant, rebuilding a chain for a value no build depends on. Both replay.

nix.detail: A variable reaches a build only as an attribute, which keys it.

cases.title: A variable both a dependency and its dependant declare reruns both when it changes
cases.why: When a value shapes both builds, both results are stale after it moves. The dependant must not replay on the grounds that its own files did not change. Both run and the dependant holds the new value.

cases.title: An input `g/a*/**` keys files under every directory starting with `a`, and no other

cases.why: A failure is never saved to the cache, so a task that failed did not replay. Turborepo’s run summary records a failed task as a miss with its exit code. A report of hit on a failure points the user at the cache instead of at the code.

cases.title: A task that passes on its second attempt reports a miss
cases.why: A retry runs the command again; nothing was replayed. A task that failed, retried and passed ran twice and its report says miss. A tool that reports the retried attempt as a hit, because the first attempt ran the same key, hides a flaky task.

turbo.detail: Turborepo does not retry a failed task.

nx.detail: Nx does not retry a failed task.

vite-task.detail: Vite Task does not retry a failed task.

nix.detail: Nix does not retry a failed build.

cases.title: A task stopped by its time limit reports a miss
cases.why: A task killed for running too long ran, and failed. Nothing was replayed and nothing saved. Its report says miss; a missing or hit status hides the hang from the person reading the report.

turbo.detail: Turborepo has no per-task time limit.

nx.detail: Nx has no per-task time limit.

vite-task.detail: Vite Task has no per-task time limit.

nix.detail: Nix has no time limit of a build’s own (`timeout` is a setting for every build).

cases.title: A dependency with caching off reports a miss while its dependant replays
cases.why: A task that is never cached runs every time, even when everything after it replays. Its report says miss beside the dependant’s hit. A tool that reports the whole chain from the dependant’s status shows a replay that did not happen.

cases.title: A task that sleeps for a second reports about a second, not much more
cases.why: A duration is useful only if it is the task’s own. A one second task reports at least a second and well under three. A tool that adds its own startup, hashing or the whole run’s time reports a number nobody can tune with.

vite-task.detail: `vp run --last-details` names the time a hit saved, never how long a task took in this run.

nix.detail: nix-build lists the derivations it builds, never how long one took.

cases.title: A task that does nothing reports a short time
cases.why: A task whose command returns at once costs almost nothing. Its report must say so, not include the runner’s own setup. Nx measures its per-task process start; a tool whose overhead lands in the task’s time makes every small task look slow.

vite-task.detail: `vp run --last-details` names the time a hit saved, never how long a task took in this run.

nix.detail: nix-build lists the derivations it builds, never how long one took.

cases.title: Two tasks running at once each report their own time
cases.why: Tasks that run in parallel overlap in time but each has its own duration. The short one reports its short time even though the long one was still running. A tool that stamps every task with the end of the slowest one hides which task is slow.

vite-task.detail: `vp run --last-details` names the time a hit saved, never how long a task took in this run.

nix.detail: nix-build lists the derivations it builds, never how long one took.

cases.title: The long task of two running at once reports its full time
cases.why: The other half of overlap: the long task’s duration is its own span, not cut short when the short task ends. A tool that measures from the last task’s end, or splits the run’s time between tasks, reports the slow one as fast.

vite-task.detail: `vp run --last-details` names the time a hit saved, never how long a task took in this run.

nix.detail: nix-build lists the derivations it builds, never how long one took.

cases.title: A task that waited for a free slot reports only the time it ran
cases.why: With one slot, the second of two independent tasks waits for the first. That wait is the queue’s, not the task’s. A tool that times from when the task was scheduled reports the queue as work and makes a concurrency limit look like a slow task.

vite-task.detail: `vp run --last-details` names the time a hit saved, never how long a task took in this run.

nix.detail: nix-build lists the derivations it builds, never how long one took.

cases.title: Both tasks that ran one after another under one slot report about their own time
cases.why: Whichever of the two tasks ran second waited a second before it started. Its report still says about a second. Checking both makes sure the tool does not report the second one as two seconds, whatever order it picked.

nix.detail: nix-build lists the derivations it builds, never how long one took.

cases.title: A task held back by a mutex reports only the time it ran
cases.why: Tasks sharing a mutex run one at a time, so one of them waits. The wait is not the task’s duration. A report that folds it in makes a task look slow because of a lock it had no part in holding.

cases.title: A workspace package with no version field builds

cases.title: A workspace package whose version is not semver builds

cases.title: A task listed twice in dependsOn runs once, before its dependant
cases.why: A list built by spreading two shared presets often names a task twice. It is one edge, and the task runs once. A tool that schedules each entry runs it twice, racing two writers into one output, or refuses a harmless list.

cases.title: `gen` and `a#gen` in one dependsOn run the task once
cases.why: Inside project `a`, `gen` and `a#gen` name the same task. A tool that dedups entries by their text, not by what they resolve to, runs it twice. It runs once, before the build.

cases.title: `a#gen` in project a’s own dependsOn runs its gen first
cases.why: A project may name its own task the long way, as a generated config does. It is the same edge as `gen`. A tool that reads `project#task` only as a cross-project edge may refuse it or skip it; gen runs first.

cases.title: `^build` and `lib#build` in one dependsOn build the library once
cases.why: When `app` depends on `lib`, `^build` and `lib#build` both reach lib’s build. It is one task, run once, before the app. A tool that adds an edge per entry builds lib twice, the second time racing the app that reads it.

cases.title: A task naming itself as `a#build` in its own dependsOn fails the run
cases.why: A task cannot finish before it starts. Spelled with its project, the self-edge goes through the cross-project lookup, which a tool may not check for cycles. Waiting on itself hangs, and skipping the edge hides a typo; the run fails before anything starts.
