cases.title: Packing the repository with `git gc` keeps the task replaying
cases.why: Git moves loose objects into packs on its own schedule; the files and their contents do not change. A tool that keys files by where git stores them, not by what they hold, loses every entry after a gc. The run after the gc replays.

cases.title: Amending the last commit’s message keeps the task replaying
cases.why: An amend makes a new commit with the same files. Nothing a task reads has changed, so its key must not either. A tool that folds the commit into the key rebuilds after every amend or rebase. The run after the amend replays.

cases.title: With a stale `.git/index.lock` left behind, a same-size edit still runs the task again
cases.why: A crashed git or editor plugin can leave `index.lock` behind, and git then refuses to write the index. A tool that needs to refresh the index to see an edit misses it, or fails the run. The run must go on and key the edited bytes.

cases.title: With `.git/index` deleted, an edit still runs the task again
cases.why: Without its index git sees every file as untracked: nothing is clean, so nothing may be keyed from git’s record. A tool that keeps trusting old facts about the files replays a stale build. The edit runs the task again and the output holds it.

cases.title: Two projects with the same command and the same sources never replay each other’s results
cases.why: Copy-pasted packages often hold byte-identical sources, yet a build can depend on where it runs, its directory name or its package. A key built only from the command and the file contents gives both one entry, and the second project replays the first one’s output. Each project builds its own.

cases.title: With git’s index in format version 4, the task replays and an edit runs it again
cases.why: Version 4 compresses paths in the index, and `feature.manyFiles` turns it on in big repositories. A tool that parses the index itself and does not know the format mis-reads every entry. Both directions must hold: replay when nothing changed, run when a file did.

cases.title: With a split git index, the task replays and an edit runs it again
cases.why: A split index keeps most entries in a shared file beside `.git/index`, which then lists only what changed. A tool that reads `.git/index` alone sees almost no tracked files. Replays and reruns must be the same as with a plain index.

cases.title: With git’s untracked cache on, a new untracked input still runs the task again
cases.why: The untracked cache lets git skip directories whose stat looks unchanged when it lists untracked files. A new file in an input directory must still be seen. A tool that trusts a stale listing replays a build without the file.

cases.title: In a git repository using SHA-256 object names, the task replays and an edit runs it again
cases.why: Git can name objects by SHA-256 instead of SHA-1, and their names are 64 hex digits, not 40. A tool that parses object names or the index with SHA-1 sizes mis-reads every entry. Caching must work as in any repository.

cases.why: The loop’s last `read` fails at the end of the file; that ends the loop and, by POSIX, does not trip `set -e`. A shell that treats it as a failure stops the command right after the loop. Every line is read and the step after the loop runs.

cases.title: A script whose shebang names an interpreter by a path over 150 bytes long runs
cases.why: Deep install directories, as Nix or a CI cache leaves them, give interpreters long paths, and Linux reads up to 255 bytes of a shebang. A runner that wraps or traces exec and cuts the line shorter starts the wrong program or none. The script runs and prints its line.

cases.title: A task that also copies a file beside the workspace through `..` is still cached
cases.why: Deploy steps copy a build into a sibling directory (`cp -r dist ../site`). What lands outside the workspace is no output, but it does not make the task uncacheable either. A tool that fails to store a task over such a path rebuilds it every run. The second run replays.

cases.title: A task killed at its time limit stops a fail-fast run like any failure
cases.why: A time limit turns a hang into a failure, and fail-fast must treat it as one. A run that stops at exit codes but not at timeouts keeps every other task running after the first one hung. The slow task is stopped before it writes its file.

cases.title: Changing only the second of two declared variables runs the task again
cases.why: Each declared variable is an input of its own, not just the first one listed. A key that folds the first value and stops, or folds only names, sees nothing new when the second value moves. The task then replays output made with the old value of a variable it reads.

cases.title: Declaring a variable the task already reads gives it the value on the next run
cases.why: Before the variable is declared, a strict tool hides it and a loose one lets it through unkeyed, so the first build may hold either value. Once it is declared, the task reads it and its value keys the result. The next run must leave the value now set, not replay a build made while the variable was hidden.

cases.title: Declaring `API` does not key the task on `API_URL`
cases.why: A declared name is the one variable it spells. A tool that matches it as a prefix keys the task on every variable that starts the same, which in CI includes values that change on each job. The task then never replays, though nothing it reads has changed.

cases.title: A declared value of `undefined` or `null` is not the same as the variable unset
cases.why: A runner written in JavaScript reads a missing variable as `undefined`, and turning that into text keys it exactly like a variable set to the word `undefined`. A shell script sees the difference at once. Keying them alike replays the unset build when the value is the word, or the reverse.

cases.title: A declared value holding `$HOME`, `${PATH}` and `$(id)` reaches the task as written
cases.why: A value is data: passwords, templates and URLs hold dollar signs and backticks. A runner that expands them, as a shell would on a command line, hands the task a different value from the one the user set and keyed. Changing only the text after a dollar must still run the task again.

cases.title: A declared value holding a backslash and `n` is not the same as one holding a newline
cases.why: Two characters, a backslash and an `n`, are not one newline, and a task reading the value sees the difference. A key built by escaping values into text and unescaping them somewhere along the way can fold the two together. The second run then replays output made from the other value.

cases.title: A value that spells out a second variable does not key like that variable set
cases.why: A key that joins `NAME=value` lines can be fooled by a value holding a newline and `B_VAL=2`: the joined text matches the run where `B_VAL` really is 2. The task sees two different environments, so the results differ. A replay across them leaves a build for variables that were never set that way.

cases.title: Changing the last of 120 declared variables runs the task again
cases.why: Large builds declare dozens of variables: feature flags, endpoints, build ids. A key that caps how many it folds, or a buffer that cuts the list short, misses a change near the end. The task then replays output made with a value it no longer has.

cases.title: A declared variable with a 241-character name reaches the task and keys it
cases.why: Generated names, such as a package scope turned into a variable, can be long. A runner that cuts names to a fixed length passes or keys a different variable, or none. The value must reach the task and a change to it must run the task again.

cases.title: With PATH declared, pointing it at another copy of a program runs the task with that copy
cases.why: PATH is usually left out of keys because it differs between machines, but a user who declares it says the task depends on which programs it finds. A tool that drops PATH from the key, or rewrites it before the task starts, replays the build made with the old program. The new PATH must both reach the task and key it.

cases.title: A variable a dependency passes through but its dependant declares reruns only the dependant
cases.why: Each task says for itself what keys it. The dependency only lets the variable through, so a change replays it; the dependant reads and declares it, so the same change runs it again. A tool that applies one task’s choice to the other either rebuilds the dependency for nothing or replays the dependant with a value it no longer has.

cases.title: A variable passed through but not set reaches the task as unset, not empty
cases.why: Passing a variable through means the task gets whatever the shell has, and here the shell has nothing. A runner that fills in an empty value for each listed name changes what `${VAR-default}` and `[ -n "${VAR+x}" ]` see. Scripts then take the empty branch, though the user set nothing.

cases.title: A variable both declared and passed through still runs the task again when it changes
cases.why: Listing a variable as passed through says it may reach the task; declaring it says its value keys the result. Both together must still key, or the declaration is silently dropped. A tool that lets the pass-through entry win replays output made with the old value.

cases.title: Output files named `a*b`, `q?`, `[x]`, `{a,b}` and `!neg` come back as written
cases.why: Output patterns are globs, but the files they match are names, and route-based frameworks write names with brackets and braces. A restore that feeds stored names back through a glob matcher can skip them, expand them or write a different file. Each one must come back under its own name.

cases.title: Output files named `-rf`, `--help`, `~`, `#x`, `%2F` and `a:b` come back as written
cases.why: A name can look like a command-line option, a home directory, a comment or a URL escape. A restore that hands names to a program, expands a `~` or decodes `%2F` into a slash writes the wrong path or none. These are ordinary file names and must round-trip unchanged.

cases.title: Output files named `...`, `..foo`, `b.` and ` lead `, spaces kept, come back
cases.why: A restore must refuse `..` as a path step, but a name that only starts with dots, or is three dots, is an ordinary file. Windows habits strip a trailing dot or space, which changes the name on Linux. A sanitizer that is too eager drops these files from the hit, and the replayed tree is short.

cases.title: Outputs `README.md`, `Readme.md` and `readme.md` all come back, each with its own bytes
cases.why: On Linux these are three files. A store that keys entries by a lowercased path, or restores through a case-insensitive map, keeps one and writes it three times or drops two. The hit must leave the three files the build wrote.

cases.title: An output whose name is exactly 100 bytes long comes back whole
cases.why: A tar header holds a name in 100 bytes, NUL-terminated only when shorter. A reader that always looks for the NUL runs into the next field and invents a longer name, and a writer can cut the last byte. Exactly 100 bytes is the edge either bug falls off.

cases.title: An output whose name is 255 bytes long, the file system’s limit, comes back
cases.why: Generated names, such as hashed chunk files, can sit right at the 255-byte limit. A store that adds a suffix while writing, such as a temporary `.tmp`, cannot create the file there and the restore fails. The file must come back under its full name.

cases.title: Output paths of 150 to 260 bytes, split at every place a tar header can split them, come back
cases.why: A tar header can hold a path of up to 255 bytes by splitting it at a slash into a prefix and a name. Paths just under, at and over that limit take different branches, and each one has had off-by-one bugs. Every path must come back exactly where the build put it.

cases.title: An output named with 40 three-byte characters, 120 bytes but 40 letters, comes back
cases.why: Header limits count bytes, and a name of CJK letters is three times as long in bytes as it looks. A writer that checks the length in characters thinks it fits and cuts it in the middle of a character. The hit then writes a name that is not even valid UTF-8.

cases.title: An output link whose target is exactly 100 bytes comes back pointing at the same name
cases.why: A tar header holds a link target in 100 bytes, with no NUL when it fills them. A reader that runs past the field points the link somewhere else; a writer that cuts a byte leaves it dangling. Exactly 100 bytes is where both happen.

cases.title: Output files of 0, 1, 511, 512, 513, 10,240 and 10,241 bytes come back at their exact sizes
cases.why: Archives pad each file to 512-byte blocks and group blocks into 10 KiB records. A reader that gets the padding wrong at the edge adds stray bytes, drops the last block or reads the next header as data. Every size at an edge must come back byte for byte.

cases.title: Two output names hard-linked to one file both come back with its bytes
cases.why: Bundlers and package tools hard-link identical files to save space. An archive may record the second name as a link to the first, and a restore that refuses or skips such entries leaves one name missing. Both names must come back holding the same bytes.

cases.title: An output file a user replaced with a link elsewhere is put back as a file, the link’s target untouched
cases.why: A restore that opens the output path and writes into it follows a link standing there, and overwrites whatever the link points at. That can be any file in the workspace or beyond. The restore must replace the link with the output file and leave the target as it was.

cases.title: One output deleted from twenty comes back on the next run, the others untouched
cases.why: A tool that decides outputs are in place by checking the directory, or a sample of files, misses one deleted file and replays nothing. Whatever needs that file then fails though the run said the task was current. The next run must put the missing file back.

cases.title: An output directory the user emptied and left in place is filled again on the next run
cases.why: An empty `dist` exists, so a check that only asks whether the output directory is there finds it and restores nothing. The files the task wrote are all gone, and the next step fails. The run must notice and bring them back.

cases.title: A program a dependency built, deleted and replayed, still runs for the dependant that calls it
cases.why: The point of restoring an executable is that it can be run. A hit that brings the file back without its executable bit, or with a broken first line, passes a file check and fails the dependant with “permission denied”. The dependant must run the replayed program as it ran the built one.

cases.title: Outputs named `café` in composed and in decomposed Unicode both come back
cases.why: Linux keeps names as bytes, so `é` as one code point and as `e` plus an accent are two files. A store that normalizes names folds them into one, restoring a single file or writing one over the other. The hit must leave both, each with its own bytes.

cases.title: Output names holding a zero-width space, a right-to-left mark or a byte-order mark come back
cases.why: These code points are valid in a name and turn up in files generated from user text. A store that strips invisible characters, or a byte-order mark at the start of a name, writes a different name or merges two. Each file must come back with its name byte for byte.

cases.title: A 64 MiB output of zero bytes comes back whole
cases.why: Zero-filled images and sparse data compress to almost nothing. A restore that guards against compression bombs by capping the expansion ratio refuses a legitimate entry, and one that streams it wrong stops short. The file must come back at its full size and bytes.

cases.title: An output whose modification time is in 1960 is cached and comes back
cases.why: Reproducible builds pin file times, and some pin them to odd dates. A time before 1970 is negative, which plain octal tar fields cannot hold. A store that fails on it caches nothing for the build, and one that misreads it may refuse the restore.

cases.title: An output whose modification time is in the year 2300 is cached and comes back
cases.why: The octal time field of a tar header runs out in 2242, after which a writer must switch to a binary form. A clock set wrong or a pinned far-future time puts such a file in the outputs. A store that overflows the field writes a broken header, and the restore fails or brings back garbage.

cases.title: An output directory named `out dir` is cached and comes back
cases.why: A space in a declared output path is part of the name, not a separator. A tool that splits the pattern on spaces looks for `out` and `dir`, saves nothing, and fails or replays an empty tree. The directory must round-trip like any other.

cases.title: An output pattern `出力/**` stores and restores the directory it names
cases.why: Teams name directories in their own language, and the output pattern names them the same way. A glob matcher that handles only ASCII matches nothing, so the task saves an empty entry or fails. The directory must come back with its files.

cases.title: A dependency’s output edited by hand is put back before the dependant that reads it rebuilds
cases.why: A dependant builds from what its dependency left on disk. If the dependency replays without restoring its edited output, the dependant reads the edit and bakes it into a fresh build that is then cached. The dependency’s outputs must hold the stored bytes before the dependant starts.

cases.title: An output file 100 directories deep comes back
cases.why: Generated trees can nest deeply, such as a copied `node_modules` or a docs site mirroring routes. A restore that walks directories recursively, or makes parents one call per level with a fixed limit, can stop partway. The file must come back at its full depth.

cases.title: Outputs `ab.txt`, `ab-c`, `ab/x` and `ab0/y` all come back, each in its place
cases.why: Sorting puts `ab-c`, `ab.txt`, `ab/` and `ab0/` in different orders depending on whether `/` sorts as a byte or as a separator. A restore that groups entries by prefix, or decides a directory is done when the next name starts differently, drops or misplaces one. Every name must land where the build put it.

cases.title: Output names holding a carriage return, a tab or an escape byte come back
cases.why: Any byte but `/` and NUL may appear in a Linux name. A store that cleans names for display, or a format that ends a record on a carriage return, writes a different name or none. The files must come back with the names the build gave them.

cases.title: Outputs named `@LongLink`, `PaxHeaders.0/x` and `GlobalHead.0.0` come back as plain files
cases.why: GNU and pax archives mark their long-name and attribute records with names like these. A reader that matches on the name instead of the record type takes a user’s file for a header and skips it, or applies it to the next entry. The build’s files must come back as files.

cases.title: An output tree of a thousand symlinks comes back with every link and its target
cases.why: Package managers lay out installs as thousands of links into a store. A restore that handles links one slow way, or caps how many it makes, leaves the tree half linked. Every link must come back with its target text.

cases.title: With `A.txt` and `a.txt` both committed, an edit to `a.txt` runs the task again
cases.why: On a case-sensitive file system `A.txt` and `a.txt` are two files with their own bytes. A runner that folds case while listing or keying them keeps only one, and an edit to the other changes no key. The task then replays output built from the old `a.txt`. Linux checkouts hold such pairs, often by accident from a rename.

cases.title: A new `a.txt` beside a committed `A.txt` runs the task again
cases.why: A new file is a new input even when its name differs from a tracked one only in case. A runner that matches new paths against tracked ones without regard to case takes `a.txt` for `A.txt`, sees nothing new and replays. The output then lacks the new file. On a case-sensitive disk the two names are as different as any others.

cases.title: An input `src/**` does not key files under a sibling `Src` directory
cases.why: Directory names are matched as exactly as file names. `Src` is another directory, maybe old code or a vendored copy, and the task does not read it. A walker that folds case pulls it into the key, so edits there rerun the task. On a case-sensitive file system the user can rely on the case they wrote.

cases.title: An input `src/[A-Z].txt` keys `B.txt`, and not `b.txt`
cases.why: A range in a class covers the characters between its ends and no others. `[A-Z]` is the upper-case letters, so `b.txt` lies outside it. A matcher that compiles classes case-insensitively keys files the user left out, rerunning the task on their edits. The upper-case file must still key the task.

cases.title: An edit to a committed file whose name is in decomposed Unicode runs the task again
cases.why: A name like `é.txt` can be stored as one code point or as `e` plus a combining accent, and files copied from macOS often carry the second form. Linux keeps the bytes as written. A runner that normalises names while listing them then looks up a path that does not exist and drops the file from the key. Its edits replay the old output.

cases.title: A new untracked file whose name is in decomposed Unicode runs the task again
cases.why: Git lists an untracked name by its bytes, and a decomposed `é` is three bytes where the composed one is two. A runner that normalises what git prints, or quotes it and fails to unquote it, never finds the file. The new input then changes no key. The task must rerun and see it.

cases.title: With composed and decomposed `é.txt` side by side, an edit to either runs the task again
cases.why: On Linux the two spellings of `é.txt` are two files with their own content. A runner that normalises names folds them into one entry, so an edit to the one it dropped changes no key. The task reads both and its output depends on both. Each must key it.

cases.title: A literal input spelled in decomposed Unicode keys the file of that spelling
cases.why: A config written on macOS may spell a name in decomposed form, and the file on disk has the same bytes. A runner that normalises the pattern but not the disk, or the other way round, matches nothing. The file then drops out of the key and its edits replay. Bytes that agree must match.

cases.title: An input `src/?.txt` keys a file named with one emoji

A matcher that steps through UTF-16 code units sees two halves and fails the match. The file then drops out of the key, and its edits replay a stale result. Emoji names are rare but legal.

A runner that passes inputs through gitignore-style parsing drops this one, and its edits replay. The pattern names a file and must key it.

cases.title: An edit to `src/!x.txt` under an input `src/**` runs the task again
cases.why: A file may begin with `!`; only a pattern starting with `!` is a negation. A runner that turns the files it found back into patterns, or prints and re-reads them, takes this name for a negation and loses it. Its edits then replay output built from the old bytes. File names are data, not syntax.

cases.title: An edit to a file whose name ends in a space runs the task again
cases.why: A name may end in a space, and such files turn up from careless saves on any system. Ignore-file parsing and line trimming both strip it, after which the runner looks up a different name and drops the file. Its edits then change no key. A file the glob matches must stay in the key with its exact name.

cases.title: An edit to a file whose name starts with a space runs the task again
cases.why: Git prints a name starting with a space as is, right after a status column. A runner that trims each line or splits on runs of white space drops the space and looks up a file that does not exist. The real file then drops out of the key. Its edits must still run the task.

cases.title: A new untracked file whose name ends in a space runs the task again
cases.why: Untracked files reach a runner through git’s status listing, where a trailing space is easy to lose. A runner that trims the line keys a name that does not exist, or none at all. The new file is a real input the task reads. It must run the task again.

cases.title: An input `src/a.txt` does not key a file named `src/aXtxt`
cases.why: In a glob a `.` is a dot. A matcher that builds a regular expression without escaping it lets the dot match any character. Files the user never named then key the task, and their edits rerun it. A literal file input must match only itself.

cases.title: An input `src/a+.txt` keys `a+.txt`, and not `aa.txt`
cases.why: Outside extended globs `+` is a plain character. A matcher that leaks it into a regular expression reads `a+` as one or more `a`, keying `aa.txt` too. That reruns the task on files it does not read. The named file must still key it.

cases.title: An input `src/$id^.txt` keys the file with `$` and `^` in its name
cases.why: Route files such as `$id.tsx` are common, and `^` is a legal name character. In a glob both are plain characters, but in a regular expression they anchor the match, so a leaked pattern matches nothing. The file then drops out of the key. Its edits must run the task.

cases.title: An edit to an input with a 250-character name runs the task again
cases.why: File systems allow names up to 255 bytes, and generated files reach that length. A runner that truncates names or builds a fixed-size buffer for them loses the file. Its edits then change no key. A long name is still a name.

cases.title: An edit forty directories deep under `src/**` runs the task again
cases.why: `**` matches any number of directories, with no depth limit. A walker that caps its recursion stops short and silently leaves deep files out. Their edits then replay a stale result. Generated trees and nested fixtures can be that deep.

cases.title: Deleting an empty input file runs the task again
cases.why: An empty file and no file are different inputs: a task can test whether the file exists. A runner that keys only file contents sees the same nothing before and after, and replays. Marker files such as `.nojekyll` are empty by design. Removing one must run the task.

cases.title: Deleting one of two inputs with the same content runs the task again
cases.why: Two files can hold the same bytes. A runner that keys the set of contents rather than each path with its content sees no change when one copy goes. The task, which reads both, would replay output that still includes the deleted copy. Each file is an input of its own.

cases.title: Adding a copy of an input under a new name runs the task again
cases.why: A new file with the same bytes as an old one is still a new input. A runner that keys only distinct blobs sees nothing new, since git stores both under one object. The task reads both and its output doubles. It must run again.

cases.title: With no line-ending rule, turning LF into CRLF runs the task again
cases.why: Without a `text` attribute or `core.autocrlf`, git stores bytes as written, and so does the task read them. A runner that normalises line endings before hashing, as some do to agree across platforms, keys both forms the same. The output, which copies the bytes, would then replay with the old endings. Different bytes are different inputs here.

cases.title: After staging an edit and undoing it on disk, the build holds the bytes on disk
cases.why: The index can hold bytes the work tree does not. A task reads the work tree, so its key must too. A runner that takes the index’s blob for a staged file replays the output built from the staged edit, though the disk went back to the first state. The output must match the disk.

cases.title: A new file staged and then deleted from disk is no input
cases.why: After `git add` and `rm`, the index lists a file the disk no longer holds. The task cannot read it. A runner that walks the index tries to hash a missing file and fails the run, or keys bytes the task never saw. The run must pass with output built from the files on disk.

cases.title: A file removed with `git rm` and written again with new bytes runs the task again
cases.why: After `git rm` the file is gone from the index, and writing it again makes it untracked with new content. A runner that reads the deletion from the index and never looks for an untracked file of that name keys the file as absent, or as its old blob. The task reads the new bytes. It must run again.

cases.title: Committing an edit and undoing the commit with `git reset --soft` lets the build replay
cases.why: `git reset --soft` moves HEAD back but keeps the edit staged and on disk. The bytes the task reads are those it was last built from. A runner that keys by HEAD’s tree sees a change and rebuilds for nothing. The disk is unchanged, so the stored result is right.

cases.title: An edit a git clean filter strips from the blob still runs the task again
cases.why: A clean filter, as nbstripout uses for notebook outputs, rewrites a file on its way into git, so an edit to the stripped part leaves the blob and `git status` unchanged. The task reads the file on disk, stripped part included. A runner that keys clean files by their blob replays output built from the old bytes. The key must follow what the task reads.

cases.title: Under the `ident` attribute, an edit inside `$Id: … $` runs the task again
cases.why: The `ident` attribute collapses `$Id: … $` back to `$Id$` when git hashes a file, so an edit inside it leaves the blob unchanged and git calls the file clean. The task reads the full text on disk. A runner keying clean files by blob replays output with the old text. What git stores is not what the task read.

cases.title: Under `status.showUntrackedFiles=no`, a new input file runs the task again
cases.why: Large repos set `status.showUntrackedFiles=no` to speed up `git status`, and plain `git status` then lists no untracked file. The new file is still on disk and the task reads it. A runner that asks status for untracked files without overriding the setting misses it and replays. A user’s status preference must not change what keys a task.

cases.title: Under `status.showUntrackedFiles=normal`, a file in a new directory runs the task again
cases.why: With `normal`, git lists a new directory as one entry, not the files inside it. A runner that keys the listed entry as if it were a file finds nothing to hash, or hashes the directory name only. Later edits inside then change no key. The files under the new directory are inputs, each with its bytes.

cases.title: Replacing an input directory with a file of the same name runs the task again
cases.why: The files under the directory are gone and a new file stands in their place. A runner that keyed the directory by the paths git listed, then fails to stat the new file as a file, can key the same before and after. The task now reads one file where it read a tree. It must run again.

cases.title: Moving an input into a new subdirectory with the same name runs the task again
cases.why: A move changes the path while the bytes stay. A runner that keys only file names, not their directories, keys `src/a.txt` and `src/sub/a.txt` alike. A task whose output depends on where files sit then replays the old layout. The path is part of each input.

cases.title: A negation `!src/*.gen.txt` does not take back `src/deep/x.gen.txt`
cases.why: A single `*` stays within one directory, in a negation as anywhere. `!src/*.gen.txt` takes back generated files at the top of `src` only. A runner that matches negations at any depth drops the deeper file, and its edits replay stale output. Only `**` reaches down.

cases.title: A negation `!src/**/*.snap` takes back snapshots at every depth
cases.why: `**` in a negation reaches every level below it, including none. Snapshot files are written by the tests, not read by the build. A runner that applies the negation only at one depth keys the rest, and every snapshot update reruns the build. The user excluded them all.

cases.title: A negation `!src/gen/**` leaves `src/gen2` keyed
cases.why: A negation of `src/gen/**` takes back the `gen` directory, whose name ends at the slash. A runner that tests negations with a string prefix also drops `gen2`, `generated` and the like. Their edits then replay stale output. Path segments are compared whole.

cases.title: A negation `!src/**/.*` takes back dotfiles and keeps the rest keyed
cases.why: Editor and tool state such as `.DS_Store` or `.eslintcache` lands beside sources, and users exclude it with a dot pattern. `.*` names files starting with a dot. A runner whose negation never matches dotfiles keys them anyway and reruns on every editor save. Ordinary files must still key the task.

cases.title: A negation `!src/[0-9]*.txt` takes back files starting with a digit only
cases.why: A class in a negation narrows it the same way as in a positive pattern. `[0-9]*.txt` names files starting with a digit, such as numbered migrations a task does not read. A runner that ignores the class keys them, or takes back too much. One must replay and the other run.

cases.title: Deleting a file a negation takes back lets the build replay
cases.why: A file the inputs take back is not keyed, so its deletion changes nothing the task reads. Deletions often reach a runner by a separate path, git’s list of removed files, and a runner that skips its negations there reruns for nothing. The stored output is still right.

cases.title: A new untracked file that a negation takes back lets the build replay

cases.title: A new file in a new directory under a negated tree lets the build replay

cases.title: A root input `.*rc` keys a dotfile at the workspace root

The task here concatenates the root files, so its output changes. It must run again.

A runner that resets the clock on each line, mixing up a time limit with an idle limit, lets that loop hold the run and the CI job for good.

cases.title: A task that sends its output to /dev/null and hangs is killed at its idle limit
cases.why: An idle limit is there to end a task that has stopped making progress. A task that points its own output at /dev/null and then hangs prints nothing from that moment, so it is idle. A runner that only watches for silence while the output pipe is open, and waits for the pipe to close otherwise, never fires the limit on it.

cases.title: A task a fail-fast run stops, which traps the stop and exits 0, is not cached
cases.why: Many programs answer SIGTERM with a clean shutdown and exit 0. When a fail-fast run stops one of them, its exit code says nothing about the work, which was cut short. Read as a success, its half-written output would be cached and replayed as a finished build on the next run.

cases.title: A retried task gets the args forwarded to the run again, each one whole
cases.why: A retry must run the same command the first attempt ran. Args forwarded to the run are part of that command: a flag, a value with a space in it. A retry that drops them, or splits them again, runs a different test than the one that failed, and its pass means nothing.

cases.title: A task given zero retries runs once and fails
cases.why: Zero retries means no retry. A runner that reads 0 as unset and falls back to some default retry count runs a failing deploy or migration again when the user said not to. The count is the number of extra attempts, and here there are none.

cases.title: A never-cached task does not run when its dependency fails
cases.why: A task that is never cached is one that must always run, such as a deploy or a smoke test. It still needs what it depends on. A runner that treats uncached tasks as always ready runs the deploy on a build that just failed.

cases.title: A cached task is not restored when the never-cached task it depends on fails
cases.why: A never-cached task, like a code generator or a fetch, can fail on a run whose inputs did not change. The task built on it has a stored result for those inputs, but its dependency just failed, so this run has nothing to build on. Restoring the stored result anyway hides the failure behind outputs that look fresh.

nix.detail: A variable reaches a build only as an attribute, which keys it.

cases.title: A task cycle in one part of the workspace fails the run before any task runs, even in parts free of it
cases.why: A graph with a cycle cannot be ordered, so the run is refused as a whole. Running the parts that happen to be free of the cycle first gives a run that is half done and still red, with outputs that look like progress. The user fixes the cycle, then runs everything.

cases.title: Turning a dependency around builds the two projects in the new order, each on the other’s fresh output
cases.why: When `b` stops depending on `a` and `a` starts depending on `b`, the order must flip. A runner that keeps an old package graph builds `a` first again, against a `b` that is not there yet. Each project’s output must reflect the new edge: replaying either old result leaves the content the wrong way round.

cases.title: A library’s build that needs a generator in the app depending on it runs in between
cases.why: The app depends on the library as a package, and the library’s build names the app’s generator. The tasks still form a straight line: generator, library build, app build. A runner that folds tasks into a project graph sees a loop between two projects and refuses a run that has a valid order.

cases.title: A workspace package named only as a dev dependency is built first, and an edit to it runs the consumer again
cases.why: A build tool, a test helper or a shared config is usually a dev dependency, and the consumer’s build reads it all the same. Whether a package ships the dependency to users changes nothing about the build order. Leaving dev dependencies out of the graph builds the consumer against a stale or missing helper.

cases.why: Inside a workspace an optional dependency is linked like any other, so the consumer’s build reads it. Optional only means an install from a registry may skip it. A runner that drops these edges builds the consumer first, or replays it after the package changed.

cases.why: Running one project runs what it depends on now, not what it used to. After the dependency is removed from the manifest, the library is just another project. A runner holding an old graph rebuilds it every time the app runs, though nothing reads it.

cases.title: A dependency renamed in both manifests still builds before the project that needs it
cases.why: Renaming a package is a common refactor, and the app’s manifest is updated to the new name in the same change. The edge is the same edge under a new name. A runner that keys its graph on the old name loses the edge and builds the app against a library that has not been rebuilt.

cases.title: Skipping dependencies runs the selected task though its dependency would fail
cases.why: Skipping dependencies is how a user reruns one task against what is already on disk, often because something below it is broken right now. The broken dependency is not part of that run. A runner that still runs it, or fails the run because of it, takes away the one way to test the task alone.

cases.why: Until the library has a build, the app’s `^build` reaches nothing there. Once it gets one, the app depends on that build: it must run first, and the app must run again on what it wrote. Replaying the app’s earlier result ships a build made before the library produced anything.

cases.title: A dependency that gains a build which fails keeps the app built on it from running or replaying
cases.why: Once the library has a build, the app depends on it, and this run’s library build failed. The app’s stored result was made before that build existed, so it says nothing about the app on top of it. Running or restoring the app hides a failure the new edge was added to catch.

cases.title: A project deleted from the workspace is no longer run, and the rest still build
cases.why: Deleting a package is an ordinary cleanup. The next run must see the workspace as it is: the remaining projects build and the deleted one is gone. A runner that keeps an old project list tries to run a task in a directory that no longer exists, or restores its outputs into a recreated folder.

cases.why: A package manager links a workspace package for any range its version satisfies, not only for `workspace:*`. Many repos predate the protocol and name siblings by version. The consumer reads the linked sibling, so the sibling must build first and its edits must run the consumer again.

cases.title: Replaying one task of a project restores its outputs and not those of the project’s other task
cases.why: A replay restores what the requested task wrote. Its sibling task was not asked for, and its outputs are not part of this run. A runner that restores everything stored for the project writes files the user just deleted on purpose, from a task that never ran.

cases.title: A check run that finds a task nondeterministic leaves the first stored result in place
cases.why: A check run is a test of the cache, not a write to it. When it finds the rebuild differs, the stored result is still what the run that saved it produced. A check that swaps in its own rebuild changes what every later run replays, as a side effect of looking.

cases.why: Adding a dependency changes what the app builds against, though none of the app’s sources changed. The new dependency must build first, and the app must run again to pick it up. Replaying the app’s old result ships a build that never saw the package the user just added.

cases.title: A project moved to another directory gets its outputs in the new directory
cases.why: After a move the project’s tasks run from its new place, and that is where their outputs belong. The runner may replay the stored result or run the task again, but the files must land under the new directory. Restoring them to the old path leaves the moved project without a build and puts files back in a directory that is gone.

cases.title: Two projects that swap directories each get their own result in their new place
cases.why: When two projects trade places, each directory now holds the other project. A runner that pairs stored results with directories restores the old occupant’s files over the new one’s sources. Whatever is replayed or rebuilt, each directory must end up with the output of the project that lives there now.

cases.title: A forced run that skips dependencies runs the selected task alone
cases.why: Forcing says ignore the cache for what this run runs; skipping dependencies says what it runs. Together they rebuild one task against what is on disk, a common way to retry a suspect build. A runner that lets the force reach the skipped dependencies rebuilds the whole chain the user left out.

cases.title: A declared value holding `%s` and `%%` reaches the task as written, and `%%` keys apart from `%`
cases.why: A value like `printf %s` or `100%%` is text, and the task must see each byte. A runner that passes values through a format function turns `%%` into `%` and fills or drops `%s`. Then two different values reach the task as one, and the cache replays one for the other.

cases.title: Declared `FORCE_COLOR` and `NO_COLOR` reach the task as the user set them, and key it
cases.why: Runners like to set colour variables themselves so that captured output stays coloured. A user who declares them has said their value matters to the task, as it does for a snapshot test of terminal output. Overriding them hands the task a value nobody set, and a change of value must still run it again.

A tool that reads it as a program named `B=two` fails the task; one that exports it hands the value to programs that should not see it. The later step expands it, and a child shell sees it unset.

cases.title: A prefix `X=hi prog "$X"` does not fill in `$X` in that same program’s args
cases.why: The shell expands a program’s words before it applies the prefix, so `X=hi echo $X` prints what `X` was before. A tool that turns the prefix into the environment of the whole line, then expands, prints `hi` where the user’s terminal prints nothing. The arg holds the value from before the prefix: unset.

cases.title: A variable exported in one step of an `&&` chain reaches the programs of the later steps
cases.why: An `export` changes the environment of the shell itself, and every program it starts afterwards inherits it. A tool that runs each step of the chain as its own process loses the export after the first step. The child shell started later sees the value.

cases.title: A `\"` inside double quotes reaches the program as a plain double quote
cases.why: Inside double quotes a backslash escapes the quote, so `"arg\"2"` is the one word `arg"2`. A tool that unquotes the command itself and ends the string at the escaped quote passes two words, or keeps the backslash. The program receives exactly `arg"2`.

cases.title: A prefix value written `FOO="BE\"R"` reaches the program as `BE"R`
cases.why: A value set in front of a program follows the same quoting as any word. A tool that lifts the prefix into an environment map with its own unquoting keeps the backslash or cuts the value at the inner quote. The program sees the value the shell would give it.

cases.title: A prefix value in quotes holding a space, `X="a b" prog`, reaches the program whole
cases.why: Quotes make `a b` one value. A tool that splits the prefix at the space sets `X=a` and runs a program named `b`. The program sees `a b`.

cases.title: Single quotes inside double quotes, and double inside single, reach the program as text
cases.why: Each kind of quote makes the other a plain character: `"hello 'world'"` and `'hello "world"'`. A tool that strips every quote it finds, of either kind, hands the program `hello world` twice. Each arg keeps its inner quotes.

cases.title: A backslash before a space, `hello\ world`, keeps the two halves one arg
cases.why: An escaped space is part of the word, the way a file name with a space is often typed. A tool that splits the command on spaces before the shell sees it passes `hello\` and `world`. The program receives one arg, `hello world`.

cases.title: Two backslashes inside double quotes reach the program as one
cases.why: Inside double quotes `\\` is an escaped backslash, so `"a\\b"` is `a\b`. A tool that unquotes without handling escapes passes both backslashes, and a Windows-style path in a task arrives doubled. The program receives a single backslash.

cases.title: An `&&`, `;`, `|` or `||` inside quotes reaches the program as text, not as a split
cases.why: A tool that splits a command at `&&` before the shell reads it must respect quotes, or a quoted script such as `node -e "a(); if (x) b()"` is cut in pieces. Inside quotes every operator is a character. The program prints the whole string.

cases.title: In `true || skip && next`, the step after `&&` still runs
cases.why: `&&` and `||` have equal precedence in `sh` and bind left to right, so the line reads `(true || skip) && next`. A tool that splits at `&&` first and then reads `||` within each part, or the other way round, runs something else. Here `skip` does not run and `next` does.

cases.title: A `!` before a program turns its failure into success, and the chain goes on
cases.why: `! grep -q x file` is how a task asserts something is absent. A tool that takes `!` as a program name, or drops it, fails the step or inverts nothing. Here the search finds nothing, so the negated step passes and the next one writes the file.

cases.title: Text after a ` #` is a comment up to the line’s end: an `&&` step written there never runs
cases.why: A comment runs to the end of the line, operators and all, and the next line is a command again. A tool that splits the command at `&&` before the shell reads it runs the commented step, here a delete. The file the first step wrote is still there, with the next line’s write after it.

cases.title: A `#` in the middle of a word, `a#b`, is text and not a comment
cases.why: Only a `#` that starts a word begins a comment. A tool that cuts the command at every `#` drops the rest of the word and everything after it. The program receives `a#b` and the step after it runs.

cases.title: A single `&` runs a step in the background, and `wait` waits for it
cases.why: One `&` starts a job without waiting; `wait` then holds the command until it ends. A tool that reads `&` as a broken `&&`, or ends the task when its shell reaches the end, loses the job’s write. The file holds what the background job wrote.

cases.title: A `{ …; }` group sends every step’s output through one redirect
cases.why: Braces group steps without a subshell, so one `>` after them catches all their output. A tool that runs the steps one by one applies the redirect to the last only. The file holds both lines.

cases.title: An `if … then … else … fi` in a command takes the branch its test picks
cases.why: Conditionals are common in tasks: build only when a file exists, pick a flag by platform. A tool that splits at `;` runs `then` and `else` as programs. The branch for the true test runs.

cases.title: An `exit 0` in the middle of a command ends it there, successfully
cases.why: `exit` ends the shell, so nothing after it runs, and the status is the one it gives. A tool that runs each step in its own shell lets the steps after it run. The run succeeds and the later write never happens.

cases.title: A step after a failure reads its status from `$?`
cases.why: In one shell, `$?` holds the status of the last command. A tool that runs the steps in separate processes, or under `set -e`, loses it or never reaches the next step. The file holds 1, the status of `false`.

cases.title: A shell function defined in a command can be called later in it
cases.why: A short function keeps a long task readable. A tool that splits the command into programs runs `greet()` as a program name. The call prints what the function says.

cases.title: A `case … esac` in a command takes the arm whose pattern matches
cases.why: `case` patterns use glob syntax and end each arm with `;;`. A tool that splits at `;` or expands the patterns against files breaks the statement. The `*.txt` arm runs.

cases.title: An arithmetic expansion, `$((6*7))`, is replaced by its value
cases.why: Tasks compute counts and ports inline. The shell evaluates `$((…))`; a tool that passes the command on without a shell, or treats the `*` as a glob, writes the text or a file list. The file holds 42.

cases.title: An unquoted glob that matches no file reaches the program as written
cases.why: In `sh`, a pattern with no match is left as it is, unlike shells set to fail or to drop it. A tool that runs commands under such a shell either fails the task or passes no argument. The program receives `src/*.nomatch`.

cases.title: A `< file` redirect feeds the file to the program’s input
cases.why: A redirect is set up by the shell before the program starts. A tool that passes `<` as an argument hands the program a file named `<`. The program reads the source and writes it upper-cased.

cases.title: A here-document with a quoted delimiter, `<<'EOF'`, keeps `$HOME` as text
cases.why: Quoting the delimiter turns off expansion inside the document, which is how a task writes a script or template holding `$`. A tool that rewrites the command, or expands variables itself, fills in the value. The file holds `$HOME` as typed.

cases.title: A command run with no forwarded args sees `$#` as 0
cases.why: A task that takes no args must not be handed any: no task name, no flag of the runner’s own. A tool that wraps the command and leaks words into its positional args changes what `"$@"` passes on. The count is 0.

cases.title: An `EXIT` trap set at the start of a command runs when the command ends
cases.why: A trap is how a task cleans up or stamps a file whatever happens. It runs when the shell exits, after the last step. A tool that runs each step in its own process never runs it. The file holds the last step’s line, then the trap’s.

cases.title: An empty quoted arg, `""`, reaches the program as an arg of its own
cases.why: Programs tell an empty value from no value: `--prefix ""` is not `--prefix`. A tool that unquotes and drops empty words shifts every arg after it. The program receives two args, the first empty.

cases.title: A `2>&1` sends the error stream down the pipe with the output
cases.why: Order matters: `2>&1 |` merges the error stream into what the next program reads. A tool that captures the error stream itself first leaves the pipe empty. The next program receives and changes the line written to the error stream.

cases.title: A backslash at the end of a line joins it to the next one
cases.why: Long commands are wrapped with `\` at the line end, and the shell reads the two lines as one. A tool that splits the command into lines first runs `two` as a program of its own. The program receives both words.

cases.title: A tab between a program and its args separates them as a space does
cases.why: The shell splits words on blanks, tabs included. A tool that splits only on spaces runs a program whose name holds a tab. The program runs with its args.

cases.title: A command that starts with blank lines and indentation still runs
cases.why: A command copied from a block string often starts with a newline and spaces. The shell skips them. A tool that takes everything before the first space as the program name runs nothing. The output is written.

cases.title: A prefix value in quotes holding `;` and `&&`, `X='a;b && c' prog`, reaches the program whole
cases.why: A tool that lifts prefixes out of the command must cut them where the shell does, not at the first operator character. Quoted, `;` and `&&` are part of the value. The program sees the whole value.

cases.title: In `a | b && c || d`, the pipe is one step whose status the `&&` and `||` act on
cases.why: A pipeline is a single step of an `&&` list: its status is its last program’s. A tool that splits at `|` before `&&` hands `c` the wrong status. Here the search fails, so the fallback runs.

cases.title: A `>` on one step of an `&&` chain catches only that step’s output
cases.why: A redirect belongs to the program it follows. A tool that splits the chain and sends the whole task’s output to the file, or that moves the redirect, writes lines the user sent to the terminal. The file holds only the first step’s line.

cases.title: A prefix value holding a glob, `X=src/*.txt prog`, reaches the program as written
cases.why: The shell does not expand file names in an assignment. A tool that expands the value itself, or treats the prefix as an arg, hands the program a file list. The program sees `src/*.txt`.

cases.title: Plain, double-quoted and single-quoted pieces with no space between them make one arg
cases.why: A word can be built from pieces quoted in different ways: `a"b c"'d e'` is the single word `ab cd e`. A tool that unquotes piece by piece and splits between them passes three args. The program receives one.

cases.title: An isolated task that hard-links an input to a name outside its outputs fails, and leaves no name
cases.why: A hard link makes a new file name, which is a write to the folder it lands in. Made outside the outputs, it is never stored and a replay leaves it out. The sandbox judges the new name like any other write: the task fails and the name is not left.

cases.why: A file’s name is part of what a task reads: a bundler emits it, a test runner reports it, a glob orders by it. Hashing only the bytes of each file, without its path, makes the renamed tree look unchanged. The task then replays a build that names the old file.

cases.title: In a workspace that is not a git repository, editing a dotfile under the inputs runs the task again
cases.why: Git lists dotfiles like any other file, so a tool keying by git sees them. A walk of the file system written by hand often skips names starting with a dot, and `.babelrc` or `.env.defaults` under the sources then never keys the task. The edit replays a build made with the old config.

cases.title: In a workspace that is not a git repository, a new empty folder under the inputs replays the task
cases.why: Input globs name files, and an empty folder adds none. With git the folder is invisible, since git tracks files only. A walk of the file system that keys directories as entries reruns the task here, so the same sources key differently with and without git.

cases.title: Making a built folder a git repository and committing it still replays the task
cases.why: A project often starts as a plain folder and becomes a repository later. Its files are the same before and after the first commit. A tool that keys tracked files by git and loose files by reading them must reach the same key both ways, or the first commit throws the whole cache away.

cases.title: A forced run under a read-only cache runs the task and leaves the stored result as it was
cases.why: A read-only cache promises not to write, and forcing the run asks only to ignore what is stored. Together the task runs and its new result goes nowhere. A tool that lets force win saves from a run that was told not to, which is how an untrusted branch overwrites the main branch’s entries.

cases.title: Two output files a task hard-linked to each other both come back on a replay
cases.why: Build tools hard-link outputs to save space: a package copied into two places, a binary under two names. An archive stores the second name as a link to the first, and a restore that skips link entries, or writes them before their target, loses one. Both names must come back with the bytes the task wrote.

cases.title: Two projects that build the same bytes get separate files: editing one leaves the other alone
cases.why: A cache that stores equal contents once may hand both projects the same file on disk. An edit to one project’s output then lands in the other project and in the stored entry too. The next replay restores the edited bytes for both, and the cache is wrong without any task running.

cases.title: Two equal output files of one task come back as separate files: editing one leaves the other alone
cases.why: Equal files in one output are common: license copies, empty markers, the same asset under two paths. A restore that writes the second as a hard link to the first ties them together, so an edit to one rewrites the other, and the stored entry too if it shares the file. The next replay must still give each its own bytes.

cases.title: An output a user replaced with a hard link to a source file is put back, and the source keeps its bytes
cases.why: A hard link is the same file under two names. A replay that opens the output and writes over it in place writes into the source file as well, destroying the user’s work without a word. Putting the output back must replace the name, leaving the other name’s bytes alone.

cases.title: A named pipe left where an output file goes is replaced by the file on the next run, without hanging
cases.why: Opening a named pipe to write it waits until something reads it, so a replay that writes over the output in place never ends. Hashing it to see whether it changed waits the same way. The run must replace the pipe with the stored file and finish.

cases.title: Swapping an input for a link to a file of the same bytes runs the task again, and swapping it back replays
cases.why: Git, a tar archive and a Nix store all record a link as a link. A task that copies, packs or lists its sources makes something different from a link than from a file, though reading through it gives the same bytes. Putting the plain file back is the first tree again, so its build replays.

cases.title: Replacing an input with a hard link to another file of the same bytes replays the task
cases.why: Deduplicating tools, package managers and backups replace equal files with hard links. The file is still a regular file with the same bytes and mode, only its inode and link count changed. A key that reads anything beyond the bytes and mode reruns the task for a tree no task can tell apart.

cases.title: A library output brought back by a replay counts as newer than the copy the app kept, so the app picks it up
cases.why: Many build steps copy or compile only what is newer than their own output, as make does. When a replay brings back an older library build, it has just been written, and the app’s copy from the newer build must count as out of date. A restore that stamps the file with the time it was first built makes the app keep the newer copy and save it under the older library’s key.

cases.title: A program a dependency built, deleted and brought back by a replay, still runs by name in its dependant
cases.why: A dependant that rebuilds while its dependency replays needs the dependency’s programs back on disk, executable, before it starts. A replay that restores the file without its mode, or after the dependant started, leaves a command not found. The dependant must run the tool just as it did when the dependency built it.

cases.title: In a workspace that is not a git repository, a folder link back into the inputs neither hangs nor fails the run
cases.why: With git the tool reads a list of files, and a link is one entry. Without git it walks the folders itself, and a walk that follows a link back to its own parent never ends. The run must key the files once and finish, and an edit must still run the task again.

cases.title: In a workspace that is not a git repository, a new file in a project that is a repository of its own runs its task again
cases.why: A vendored project often keeps its own `.git` inside a workspace that has none. A tool that finds that repository and keys the project by what it tracks misses a file nobody committed there. The new file is still an input, and the task must run again.

vx.detail: vx finds the workspace root inside a git work tree and keys tracked files by git, so a folder that is not a repository is refused.

cases.title: In a workspace that is not a git repository, editing a workspace-level file a task declares runs it again
cases.why: A shared config at the workspace root, such as a `tsconfig.base.json`, keys every task that names it. Without git the tool must find and read it outside the project’s own folder. A tool that walks only the project when git is missing replays builds made with the old config.

vx.detail: vx finds the workspace root inside a git work tree and keys tracked files by git, so a folder that is not a repository is refused.

cases.title: After a forced run writes other bytes, the next replay restores the forced run’s bytes
cases.why: A user forces a run because they no longer trust what is stored. If the task now writes something else, the stored result must become the new one. A cache that keeps the first entry for a key it already holds replays the very result the user asked to replace.

cases.why: A task’s name is the user’s label, not a statement about what it does. Names like `dev` and `start` often belong to dev servers, but here they are plain builds the user marked cacheable. cases.title: An input `src/a}{b.txt` keys the file of that name
cases.why: A `}` before any `{` closes nothing, and a `{` with no `}` after it opens nothing, so both are plain characters of the name. File names carry braces from templating tools and copied paths. A runner that rejects the pattern, or reads it as a broken alternative that matches nothing, either fails the run or replays a build of an edited file.

cases.title: Once a new dependency project is deleted again, the next run builds without it and does not bring it back
cases.why: Undoing a change is ordinary: a project added on a branch and then thrown away is gone. The run after it must plan from the workspace as it stands now. A runner that remembers the deleted project from an earlier graph either fails on a dependency that no longer exists or writes its directory back.

cases.title: A task that edits the root .gitignore and then fails still fails the run
cases.why: Tools write ignore rules: a generator adds its output folder, a setup step adds a cache directory. A change to which files git ignores is not a reason to stop judging the task’s exit code. A run that loses track of the failure and reports success lets a broken build through CI.

cases.title: Editing the patch applied to an installed package, and installing, runs the task reading it again
cases.why: A patch is part of the installed package: after the install, the files the task reads hold the patched bytes. The lockfile names the patch file but not what it says, so a key built only from the lockfile sees nothing change. The task must run again, or it replays a build of the old patch.

cases.title: A build run after a patch edit but before the install is not replayed once the install applies it
cases.why: A pull can change a patch file while the installed package still holds the old patched bytes. A build run then reads the old bytes, but the patch file it is keyed on is already the new one. Stored under that key, the old build comes back after the install, so the patch looks applied when it is not. The tool must refuse to build on the stale install, or keep that result out of the cache.

cases.title: In a git worktree under a folder the main checkout ignores, an input edit runs the task again
cases.why: Agents and scripts keep extra worktrees in a folder like `.worktrees/` that the main checkout ignores. Inside the worktree, that folder is outside the workspace, so it says nothing about which files are inputs. A tool that matches its ignores against the full path drops every input there and replays the old output after an edit. The edited input is built.

cases.title: A task that also copies its build beside the repository is cached and replays
cases.why: A build that publishes a copy to a folder beside the repository, `cp -r dist ../site`, still declares its outputs inside its project. What it writes outside is not among them, and is no reason to refuse the result. A tool that fails to save such a task builds it on every run. The run passes and the next one replays.

cases.title: An `EXIT` trap reads the status the command is leaving with in `$?`
cases.why: A cleanup trap often records or reports how the script ended, and `$?` on entry to an `EXIT` trap is that status. A shell that hands the trap 0 makes a failed build log success. The trap writes 4, and the task fails.
